detail.title: Feed input investment, grazing management and milk performance in family-based mountain dairy goat systems in Kabylia, Algeria
detail.abstract: Goat farming is a cornerstone of rural livelihoods in the mountainous region of Kabylia (Tizi-Ouzou and Bejaia, Algeria), where family-based systems depend mainly on natural rangelands, complemented by purchased feeds. This study had two objectives: first, to build a typology of goat farms based on their level of feed input investment, and second, to assess how this investment is linked to grazing practices and milk performance. We surveyed 178 farms using a structured questionnaire that captured socio-economic features, herd management, feeding practices, feed expenditure and milk yield. Feed investment profiles were derived through principal component analysis followed by Ward’s hierarchical clustering, and the determinants of investment level were explored using a mixed-effects ordinal logistic regression model. Four clearly distinct profiles emerged-Low, Medium, High and Very High feed investment-which differed markedly in herd size, daily grazing time, concentrate allocation, feed expenditure and milk yield (P < 0.0001). Farms in the Medium group produced 553 Liter/goat/lactation at a feed cost of 12,291 Algerian Dinars (AD)/goat, a performance comparable to that of the Very High group (562 L, 82,537 AD/goat), highlighting the strong efficiency of combining extended grazing (~6 hour/day) with moderate supplementation (~340 grammes/head/day). The ordinal regression indicated negative associations of feed investment with herd size and daily grazing time, whereas households whose main activity was commerce were more likely to belong to higher investment categories (P < 0.05). Natural rangelands remained the backbone of feeding strategies in all profiles. Overall, the results show that economic performance in mountain dairy goat systems is driven less by maximal concentrate use than by optimising rangeland utilisation through targeted, cost-effective supplementation, and they argue in favour of policies that focus on rangeland management, technical training and better organisation of input and product value chains rather than on blanket concentrate subsidies.

title: Gripezinha: Evidence for retrospective voting amid government misinformation
affiliations: University of Zurich and University of Reading

detail.title: Gripezinha: Evidence for retrospective voting amid government misinformation
detail.abstract: Retrospective voting underpins electoral accountability. However, recent research shows that false beliefs rooted in misinformation may obstruct retrospective voting. We therefore ask: Does retrospective voting work in a context of widespread misinformation? We address this question through the lens of the Covid-19 pandemic in Brazil. Jair Bolsonaro, president at the time, ran a massive misinformation campaign about Covid-19, coining the myth of “Gripezinha” (Engl.: small flu) – with fatal consequences. We show that voters with a larger propensity to be exposed to information about the true state of the world punished Bolsonaro more in the 2022 Presidential Election. We measure information exposure by spatial proximity to hospitals with more intensive care units (ICUs). The severity of the pandemic and the breakdown of the healthcare system became salient in those locations. The effect is sizeable: If information exposure had been 5 points lower (on a 10-point scale), the election result would have been flipped.

title: Electoral Neutrality and the Incumbency Paradox: Executive Power, Appointment Authority, and the Subversion of Political Rights in Uganda
affiliations: We Care Legal Aid Agency

detail.title: Electoral Neutrality and the Incumbency Paradox: Executive Power, Appointment Authority, and the Subversion of Political Rights in Uganda
detail.abstract: Electoral neutrality is frequently treated as an administrative or procedural concern, reducible to polling-day conduct and the technical competence of electoral management bodies. This paper rejects that narrow framing and instead conceptualizes electoral neutrality as a structural and constitutional question grounded in power, institutional design, and human rights. Using Uganda as a case study, and engaging constitutional provisions, electoral legislation, international and regional human rights treaties, and Supreme Court jurisprudence, the paper argues that where an incumbent executive remains in office throughout the electoral cycle while retaining decisive appointment authority over electoral institutions and security forces, neutrality becomes largely illusory. Executive dominance constitutionalizes incumbency advantage and normalizes elections that are formally lawful yet substantively compromised. The paper concludes that without a redistribution of executive power and a reconfiguration of appointment regimes, electoral processes may satisfy procedural legality while violating the deeper human rights norms of political equality, participation, and democratic selfdetermination.

title: Health Policy Responses To Pandemic Preparedness And Resilience
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Health Policy Responses To Pandemic Preparedness And Resilience
detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic revealed the deep-seated weaknesses in the global health systems and also reinstated the importance of preparedness and resilience as the policy priorities in addressing future health emergencies. In various parts of the world and on both low-cost and high-cost pillars, inconsistent response capacities, disrupted core services, and continued imbalances outlined the extent of responsive measures and instilled stress on forward-looking and long-term policy frameworks (Sundarararam et al., 2021; Haldane et al., 2021). It is within this backdrop that this research study will analyze how the design and implementation of health policies determine the preparedness and resilience during pandemics in various settings. In methodology, the paper takes the form of a systematic policy analysis along with a critical review of the world and regional empirical evidence, relying on comparative research, international documents, and scholarly publications to uncover recurrent patterns and determinants of policies (Mustafa et al., 2022; Maccaro et al., 2023). The analysis indicates that the quality of governance, the sustainability of health financing, and policy decisions based on equity remain the decisive issues contributing to resilient reaction to pandemics affecting coordination, trust, and coverage of services (Sagan et al., 2021; Alberti et al., 2020). Meanwhile, the evidence points to the continued fragmentation of policies, the lack of adequate intersequestration, and considerable gaps in implementation that traverse across a low-, middle-, and high-income context, and worsen preparedness, even in a setting where there are formal strategies and plans in place (Radford et al., 2024; Chavez et al., 2025). The research finds that it is not possible to maintain pandemic resilience only with technical capacity, but adaptive, equity-based, and learning-based health policies are needed that institutionalise accountability, bring evidence into decision-making, and focus on vulnerable groups. These policy orientations are essential to make preparedness commitments translate into functional and long-term level resiliency to future outbreaks associated with pandemics (Okyere et al., 2024; Lal et al., 2022).

title: Paradigm Shift from Territory to Connectivity: Introducing Corridor Economics and Its Contributions
affiliations: and University of Isfahan

detail.title: Paradigm Shift from Territory to Connectivity: Introducing Corridor Economics and Its Contributions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Conflict of Interest has been reported

detail.abstract: This paper offers Corridor Economics as a new way of understanding how contemporary economic corridors operate in the global system. Rather than viewing corridors only as physical infrastructure projects designed to move goods more efficiently, the paper argues that they have increasingly become institutional and monetary spaces where new forms of economic coordination are being tested. Corridors such as the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), etc. are not merely transport routes; they are emerging platforms for digital payments, alternative settlement mechanisms, and corridor-based governance. This shift reflects broader structural changes, including the expansion of South-South cooperation, the rapid digitization of financial systems, and the gradual weakening of dollar-centered monetary arrangements, particularly within multipolar groupings such as BRICS. On this basis, the paper introduces two theoretical innovations. The first is the Asymmetric Distance Optimum Currency Area (ADOCA) model, which revisits Robert Mundell's classical OCA (Optimum Currency Area) framework by moving beyond its emphasis on geographic proximity. Instead, it highlights the role of corridor connectivity, institutional coordination, and technological integration in shaping monetary compatibility. The second is the Ideal Global Currency (IGC) framework, inspired by John Nash's idea of Ideal Money. The IGC does not seek to replace national currencies, but rather envisions digitally anchored, corridor-based units of account that can support cross-border trade while improving stability, lowering transaction costs, and preserving monetary sovereignty. Methodologically, the paper follows a theoretical and conceptual approach. It brings together insights from monetary theory, institutional economics, digital finance, and geoeconomics, and draws on policy documents, corridor initiatives, and emerging payment systems such as CBDCs and BRICS Pay. This allows the study to show how corridors are increasingly functioning as institutional ecosystems rather than as simple trade channels. The paper makes four main contributions: it conceptualizes Corridor Economics as a distinct analytical field; it reformulates OCA theory through the ADOCA model; it translates Nash's Ideal Money into an operational framework through the IGC; and it questions the long-standing assumption that monetary integration must be based on territorial proximity or political unification. In doing so, it advances a post-territorial understanding of monetary integration grounded in connectivity, institutional trust, and digital interoperability.

title: Business Agility and Socio-Technical Resilience: An Assessment of Large-Scale Agile Frameworks

detail.abstract: In today's volatile and complex business environment, large-scale Agile frameworks (LSAFs) have emerged as pivotal enablers of organisation-wide agility, with many organisations seeking improved resilience. However, many of these frameworks were not originally designed for this purpose, raising questions about their adequacy and alignment with these multidimensional concepts. Compounding this challenge is the absence of a unified view of business agility and the dimensions of business that it encompasses, which impedes consistent assessment and benchmarking. In this study, we developed a thematic clustering of business agility dimensions derived from academic literature and practitioner perspectives (which we call domains). We also adapted Hollnagel's RAG (resilience analysis grid) for organisational resilience to apply to LSAFs. Using these instruments, we assess the extent to which widely adopted LSAFs incorporate and support business agility and resilience. A matrix-based assessment tool employing a Likert scale was developed to collect quantitative ratings and qualitative justifications, which were then analysed using descriptive statistical methods. The findings reveal substantial variability in how different frameworks address core agility domains and resilience concepts, uncovering both strengths and critical gaps. This research contributes a novel empirical framework for assessing the support for business agility and organisational resilience provided by LSAFs, offering insights for practitioners and researchers regarding the relationship between business agility and socio-technical resilience.

title: Fiscal Decentralization as a Structural Ecological Modifier: Evidence from Kenya’s Post-Devolution Biocapacity Balance
affiliations: University of Embu

detail.title: Fiscal Decentralization as a Structural Ecological Modifier: Evidence from Kenya’s Post-Devolution Biocapacity Balance
detail.abstract: Economic growth in developing economies increasingly unfolds under binding ecological constraints, yet empirical assessments of decentralization reforms continue to rely on emissions-based indicators that overlook biophysical limits. This study examines whether Kenya’s post-2013 fiscal decentralization altered the structural relationship between economic growth, population pressure, and ecological sustainability. Guided by an extended STIRPAT framework, fiscal decentralization is treated as a structural institutional shift capable of modifying environmental elasticities rather than producing direct level effects. Using annual national time-series data for 2013–2024 and estimating models with Newey–West corrected standard errors, the analysis tests both baseline and interaction specifications. Results reveal persistent ecological overshoot throughout the post-devolution period, with ecological footprint consistently exceeding domestic biocapacity despite rising incomes and relatively low emissions. Fiscal decentralization exhibits no direct environmental effect; however, interaction models show that decentralization significantly reshapes ecological elasticities. Specifically, higher fiscal decentralization amplifies the growth–ecological footprint and growth–emissions elasticities, while attenuating the per-capita ecological pressure associated with population growth. These findings are robust across alternative outcome measures, first-difference models, and exclusion of COVID-19 years. The study contributes new evidence that fiscal decentralization in biocapacity-constrained, low-emissions economies operates as a structural moderator rather than an environmental corrective. By integrating biocapacity constraints into decentralization analysis, the paper advances sustainability scholarship beyond emissions-centric and Environmental Kuznets Curve frameworks, highlighting that governance reforms interact with fixed ecological limits in non-linear and trade-off-laden ways.

detail.abstract: Home-based healthcare is a critical part of the U.S. healthcare provision system. It serves elderly individuals, people with disabilities, and patients with chronic or post-acute care needs. As reliance on in-home care increases, continuity of care is a key determinant of clinical outcomes, healthcare quality, and system sustainability. This paper investigates patient onboarding as a mechanism that influences continuity of care in U.S. home-based healthcare. Instead of viewing onboarding solely as an operational process, the study situates it within a broader framework. It emphasizes the role of onboarding in care continuity, patient engagement, care integration, patient safety, and healthcare system performance. Drawing on healthcare systems and public health literature, the analysis explores how onboarding practices affect patient engagement, care stability, and service continuity, and how these factors impact government-funded home care programs. The paper concludes with recommendations to enhance care continuity in U.S. home-based healthcare.

detail.abstract: The European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) marks a fundamental shift in global trade governance by integrating climate objectives directly into market access rules. Unlike traditional tariffs, CBAM introduces carbon-based cost adjustments and mandatory emissions reporting for selected imported goods. This paper presents a comparative analysis of CBAM's economic impact on India and China, two major developing economies with significant carbon-intensive exports to the European Union. Using secondary data, peer-reviewed literature, and sectoral exposure analysis, the study evaluates direct cost impacts, compliance burdens, competitiveness effects, and policy response capacities in both countries. The findings indicate that while China faces larger absolute exposure due to export scale and deeper integration into EU value chains, it possesses stronger institutional and financial capacity to adapt. India, though less exposed at the macroeconomic level, experiences sharper sector-specific pressures, particularly in steel and aluminium, with constraints related to emissions measurement, financing, and technological readiness. The paper concludes that CBAM functions less as a short-term tariff and more as a long-term structural filter that rewards credible low-carbon production, reshaping global trade patterns and accelerating industrial decarbonization.

title: Narrating Inflation: How German Economic Journalists explained Post-Covid Price Rises
affiliations: Institute of Journalism at TU Dortmund University

detail.title: Narrating Inflation: How German Economic Journalists explained Post-Covid Price Rises
detail.abstract: Economic narratives play a central role in shaping expectations, particularly during periods of high uncertainty. While a growing literature examines how media narratives affect economic beliefs, little is known about the journalists who articulate and/or reproduce these narratives. Using a mixed-methods design that combines survey data with media content analysis, this study investigates how German economic journalists explained inflation causes and persistence in 2022, how their views compared with those of professional economists, and how these narratives were reflected in inflation-related media coverage. The findings reveal broad alignment between journalists and economists regarding the main drivers of inflation – most notably energy shocks and supply-chain disruptions – but also systematic differences in emphasis. Journalists were more pessimistic about inflation persistence and placed greater weight on monetary policy and corporate profiteering. Narrative embedding and clustering analyses show that both groups drew on two latent narrative templates, a supply-oriented and a policy-oriented narrative, that cut across professional boundaries. Media analysis further shows that journalists’ narratives aligned more closely with 2022 inflation coverage, particularly in the prominence given to the European Central Bank. Taken together, the results suggest that economic journalism neither merely transmits expert consensus nor operates independently of it, challenging the view of the media as a mere transmission channel of monetary policy communication. Incorporating the producers of economic narratives into narrative economics offers a more complete understanding of how economic meaning is constructed in the public sphere.

title: The Fitrah Framework: A Universal Psychometric Architecture of Human Flourishing-Theoretical Foundations and Empirical Validation

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces and validates the Fitrah Framework—a universal, multi-dimensional model of human nature grounded in the Islamic philosophical concept of fitrah (primordial human disposition). In response to the reductionist and WEIRD-centric limitations of contemporary personality psychology, we propose an eight-faculty ontology comprising Physical (F1), Mental (F2), Intellectual (F3), Emotional (F4), Social (F5), Volitional (F6), Moral (F7), and Spiritual (F8) dimensions. These faculties are theorized as innate, interdependent, and cross-culturally invariant, forming the foundational "hardware" of human functioning.

We detail the development and psychometric validation of the Fitrah Scale, an 18-item instrument demonstrating high internal consistency (α = 0.853) and factorial validity across five dimensions: Beatitude, Moral Uprightness, Devoutness, Innate Goodness, and Faith in God. The framework is situated within a nomological network linking it to established models (HEXACO, VIA, leadership competencies), while highlighting its unique inclusion of Moral and Spiritual faculties as sovereign dimensions rather than peripheral concerns.

Cross-cultural validation demonstrates measurement invariance across Muslim and non-Muslim populations (n=812 across four countries), supporting the framework's universal applicability. The paper positions the Fitrah Framework as the foundational ontology for the Human Resonance Systems (HRS) model, where these eight faculties form the substrate that is both measured (via EB BCA: readiness R = P(1-DR)) and structured (via IACM: institutional authority domains). The framework offers a holistic, culturally calibrated foundation for the science of human development, well-being, organizational design, and institutional effectiveness—bridging Islamic philosophical psychology with contemporary empirical research. The framework's Eight-Faculty architecture forms the measurement substrate for Evidence-Based Behavioral-Cognitive Assessment (Paper 2) and the human-centered governance model in Institutional Authority Constitutional Mechanics (Paper 3), with practical application through the Fitrah Verification Protocol for AI integration (Paper 4).

title: Unveiling Complex Biomarkers in Neurodegenerative Diseases via Robust Penalized FDR with Entropy-based Gini-Simpson Index in Graph Neural Networks

detail.title: Unveiling Complex Biomarkers in Neurodegenerative Diseases via Robust Penalized FDR with Entropy-based Gini-Simpson Index in Graph Neural Networks

detail.abstract: Deciphering the molecular drivers of neurodegenerative diseases is often hindered by the "missing heritability" problem, where a substantial portion of phenotypic variance remains unexplained by identified genetic loci. Much of this missing information resides in the "dark matter of omics"-complex, non-linear regulatory dependencies that are typically obscured by measurement outliers and the high-dimensional, low sample size (HDLSS) nature of clinical cohorts. Here, we present a robust, information-theoretic framework that bridges Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with frequentist hypothesis testing to illuminate these hidden landscapes. Our approach utilizes an Entropy-based Gini-Simpson (EGS) index to transform GNN structural uncertainty into a measure of functional pleiotropy, integrated with a robust M-estimation kernel for rigorous False Discovery Rate (FDR) control. Applied to Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease multi-omics datasets, our framework achieved a 42% increase in validated biomarker recovery compared to state-of-the-art methods. Crucially, we identified a previously undetected synaptic vesicle trafficking bypass mediated by the SNARE complex, providing a novel mechanism for cognitive resilience. Furthermore, we reveal that TREM2 acts as a high-entropy diversity hub governing the homeostatic-to-neuroinflammatory microglial transition. By resolving the tension between structural complexity and statistical conservatism, this framework enables systematic therapeutic prioritization, offering a mathematical blueprint for discovering actionable targets in the complex dark matter of human disease.

title: Designing Medicines Reliance and Accelerated Access for Small Markets: A Comparative Institutional Analysis with Implications for New Zealand Author

detail.title: Designing Medicines Reliance and Accelerated Access for Small Markets: A Comparative Institutional Analysis with Implications for New Zealand Author

detail.abstract:
Background: New Zealand and other small pharmaceutical markets routinely wait months or years longer than patients in the US or Europe for access to new medicines. This “drug lag” persists not because these countries lack competent regulators, but because their agencies duplicate assessments that major authorities have already completed. Two strategies can break this cycle: regulatory reliance (formally recognizing foreign decisions) and fast-track mechanisms (accelerating approval for urgent therapies). This study examines how these tools work in practice and whether combining them offers a better path forward.

Methods: We analyzed medicines regulatory pathways across eight jurisdictions- New Zealand, Australia, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Canada, Singapore, Switzerland, and Japan- using systematic documentary analysis of 136 legislative instruments, guidance documents, and agency reports. Documents were assessed against a framework examining legal architecture, recognition rules, processing timelines, and post-market requirements.

Results: We found a spectrum of approaches. At one end, Singapore and New Zealand (proposed) use Verification- essentially validating that a trusted foreign agency has already approved a product. At the other, reference authorities like FDA and EMA conduct full independent assessments. In between, the UK uses Recognition (tiered acceptance of foreign decisions), while Australia, Canada, and Switzerland use Abridged Assessment (targeted domestic review using foreign reports as the foundation). Separately, fast-track mechanisms across jurisdictions consistently reduced approval times by 3-12 months. We found that leading small regulators don’t choose between reliance and speed- they layer them. Singapore, for instance, pairs its verification pathway with priority review for breakthrough therapies, achieving approvals in under 60 days for high-priority medicines.

Conclusion: New Zealand’s proposed “Rule of Two” (automatic approval if two trusted agencies concur) is a sensible efficiency measure but has a blind spot: breakthrough therapies often receive a single major approval first, with a second lagging by months. A rigid dual-approval requirement could paradoxically delay exactly the medicines patients need most urgently. Our analysis suggests a hybrid design: the Rule of Two as the default high-volume pathway, supplemented by a conditional access tier recognizing single approvals for innovative therapies with unmet need.

detail.abstract:
Contemporary psychometric assessments often reduce individuals to scores that obscure the full cognitive-behavioral complexity of human capacity. We present Evidence-Based Behavioral Cognitive Assessment (EB-BCA), a framework grounded in Sovereign Epistemology—the doctrine that treats individuals as sovereign epistemic agents capable of producing and evaluating truth.

EB-BCA operationalizes Readiness (R) as the product of latent Presence (P)—true capability signal—and resilience against Distortion Risk (DR): R = P × (1 − DR). This signal-to-noise model formalizes the gap between potential and reliably expressed capability, accounting for stress, bias, impression management, and other sources of distortion. 

The framework employs eight evidence engines: Evidence-Centered Design (ECD), Naturalistic Decision-Making (NDM), Logic-Density Analysis (LDA), Situational Judgment Tests (SJT), Moral Disengagement Probing (MDP), Social Baseline assessment, Item Response Theory (IRT) calibration, and Validity Dossier system.

EB-BCA operationalizes measurement within the Eight-Faculty Fitrah Framework (Paper 1), which establishes the ontological foundation for what human capacity actually is, and within institutional authority architectures (IACM, Paper 3), which determine whether and how that capacity can be authentically expressed. This yields both individual readiness diagnostics and organizational design imperatives, with practical implementation through the Fitrah Verification Protocol for AI contexts (Paper 4).

detail.abstract: Traditional competitive strategy assumes that firms operate within industries characterized by rivalry, substitution, and the threat of entry. This paper argues that a growing class of companies instead transition into substrates: foundational systems upon which markets, institutions, and decision-making processes depend. When firms reach this condition, the classical threat of new entrants ceases to operate as a meaningful competitive force-not due to monopoly power, but because entry would require recreating historical, cognitive, and institutional path dependence. This paper proposes a boundary condition on Porter's Five Forces, introducing a four-force framework governing substrate systems while leaving the original framework intact for industry contexts.

title: Redistributing Decision-Making Power and Influence in the AI Ecosystem: A Call for Inclusive Participation of Users and User Organisations

detail.title: Redistributing Decision-Making Power and Influence in the AI Ecosystem: A Call for Inclusive Participation of Users and User Organisations
detail.abstract:
Contemporary debates on artificial intelligence (AI) risk management and governance have been dominated by a narrow set of actors—namely large AI foundation model developers, government agencies, select non-governmental organisations, and academic institutions. While these actors shape the regulatory, ethical, and technical contours of the AI ecosystem, users and user organisations—corporations, non-profits, public institutions, and individual practitioners who deploy AI systems in real-world contexts—remain largely excluded from formal decision-making processes. This exclusion persists despite the fact that users generate the economic value, data, and operational contexts upon which AI systems depend.

This paper argues that the marginalisation of users from AI governance constitutes a structural imbalance of power with significant legal, ethical, and societal implications. Drawing on developments in AI regulation, fiduciary law, data rights, and risk management practices, the paper demonstrates how existing governance frameworks insufficiently address issues of consent, accountability, data appropriation, concentration of power, and downstream harms experienced by users. It further highlights the growing misalignment between the expanding societal deployment of AI systems and the limited participation of affected stakeholders in defining acceptable risk thresholds and governance norms.

The paper advances a normative and institutional case for inclusive AI governance, calling for the formal incorporation of users and user organisations into AI risk management, policy formulation, ethical standard-setting, and oversight mechanisms. It outlines practical pathways for achieving such inclusion, including strengthened legal rights, participatory governance processes, fiduciary accountability, external auditing, and user-driven internal AI governance frameworks. The paper concludes that redistributing decision-making power within the AI ecosystem is not merely a matter of fairness, but a structural necessity to ensure legitimacy, trust, and long-term sustainability in AI governance.

detail.abstract: In the context of accelerated cultivation of new quality productive forces, the cultural industry-a strategic sector that combines economic value with cultural attributes-has been entrusted with the mission of creating new growth drivers and strengthening national soft power. Compared with macro-level industrial planning and capital operations, the highquality development of the cultural industry is more directly reflected in frontline practitioners' forms of work, career development, and quality of life. Through technological iteration, institutional innovation, and factor recombination, new quality productive forces have reshaped the production and value chains of cultural products, profoundly altering practitioners' occupational roles, skill structures, and labor relations. On the one hand, the diffusion of digital technologies and cross-sector integration such as "culture + technology", "culture + tourism", and "culture + finance" have created abundant job demand and diversified career pathways; on the other hand, the expansion of project-based and platform-based employment, algorithm-driven traffic competition, pressures for continuous upskilling, and rising intensity of emotional labor have exposed practitioners to multiple challenges including employment instability, income volatility, and heavy physical and psychological stress. Building on a review of the interaction mechanisms between new quality productive forces and the cultural industry, this paper analyzes the opportunities and challenges brought to cultural industry practitioners from the perspective of labor and occupation, and proposes response approaches at four levels-government, industry organizations, cultural enterprises, and individuals-to provide references for promoting high-quality development of the cultural industry and realizing decent work for practitioners.

detail.abstract: On October 25, 2021, Nigeria joined the list of countries and became the first country in Africa to introduce a digital currency with the launch of the eNaira. The eNaira is touted as a 'game changer' that will transform commerce in the continent's largest economy, cut transaction costs, boost cross-border trade, improve monetary policy, and financial inclusion. Just as the eNaira serves these purposes, so do several cryptocurrencies. However, unlike the former, the latter is accompanied by several regulatory difficulties in Nigeria, to the extent that Banks and Other financial institutions are prohibited from dealing in cryptocurrency transactions. This is primarily because cryptocurrencies are susceptible to illicit uses, such as money laundering, terrorism financing, and volatility, as well as the presence of anonymity. Nonetheless, some jurisdictions have adopted cryptocurrency as a legal tender due to its benefits. Premised on the aforesaid, this thesis chiefly concerns itself with the regulatory framework for fiat currencies in Nigeria and the issues surrounding digital currencies. It primarily seeks to explore the regulatory state of digital tenders in Nigeria, and it juxtaposes it with other advanced jurisdictions. The purpose is to determine the state of cryptocurrencies in these jurisdictions and the possibility of a regulatory framework in Nigeria. Complementary to this primary goal, this thesis examines the nature of cryptocurrencies, highlighting their benefits and shortcomings, and juxtaposes them with fiat currencies. It also examines the challenges to the successful adoption of cryptocurrency in Nigeria. The thesis finds that Nigeria may need to research how other jurisdictions have successfully adopted cryptocurrency despite its numerous challenges. Harmonizing the benefits and challenges of cryptocurrency adoption, the thesis concludes with a proposed regulatory framework for adopting cryptocurrency in Nigeria.

title: American Pandemic Options under a Stochastic SIR Model with Degenerate Diffusion
affiliations: Tokyo University of Science - Department of Industrial Administration, Tokyo University of Science, Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology and Faculty of Economics, Ryukoku University

detail.title: American Pandemic Options under a Stochastic SIR Model with Degenerate Diffusion
detail.abstract: We computationally study the valuation of American-style contingent claims written on epidemic indicators under a stochastic Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered (SIR) model with degenerate diffusion. The epidemic dynamics evolve on a constrained triangular state space induced by population conservation, where the diffusion coefficient vanishes along the boundary corresponding to the exhaustion of susceptible individuals. This structural degeneracy gives rise to a nonlinear free-boundary problem formulated as a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman variational inequality. We first establish the well-posedness of the stochastic SIR model by proving the existence, uniqueness, and positivity of solutions, and derive conditions. The American pandemic call option is then formulated as an optimal stopping problem, leading to a variational inequality defined on the triangular domain. Our primary contribution lies in a coordinate transformation that aligns the degenerate diagonal boundary with the computational grid, reducing numerical instability and enabling a consistent treatment of boundary transport dynamics. Numerical experiments show that the option value is concave with respect to the infectious population, reflecting the saturation effect inherent in SIR dynamics. Furthermore, we find that higher volatility creates a trade-off between two opposing effects: it suppresses the epidemic's growth potential on one hand, while simultaneously supporting the option value through financial convexity on the other.

title: Suitable Site Selection of Mariculture Floating Cages in the Egyptian Mediterranean Coast Using Geomatics and Remote Sensing

detail.title: Suitable Site Selection of Mariculture Floating Cages in the Egyptian Mediterranean Coast Using Geomatics and Remote Sensing
detail.abstract: The sustainable expansion of mariculture along the western Egyptian Mediterranean coast requires a spatially informed understanding of environmental and operational constraints to ensure optimal site for floating cage system. This study presents an integrated geospatial framework for identifying suitable locations for floating cage mariculture along the western Egyptian Mediterranean coast between Al-Sallum and Marsa Matrouh. Remote sensing data, oceanographic reanalysis products, national geospatial datasets and in situ water quality measurements were combined within a GIS based multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) environment. Key environmental and operational criteria including bathymetry, current velocity, wind speed, sea surface temperature, chlorophyll-a, turbidity, salinity, total dissolved solids, ammonia, dissolved oxygen, proximity to ports and marine protected areas were standardized using ecologically relevant thresholds. The Analytic hierarchy process (AHP) was applied to derive criterion weights with bathymetry (0.214) and current velocity (0.173) identified as the most influential factors. A weighted overlay analysis was then used to generate a comprehensive mariculture suitability map. The results indicate that 19.44% of the study area is highly suitable for floating cage mariculture, 22.94% is moderately suitable, 8.69% is of low suitability and 48.93% is unsuitable due to environmental, operational or regulatory constraints. Marsa Matrouh emerged as the most favorable site for large scale mariculture development followed by Al-Sallum and Sidi Barani based on combined suitability scores, available area, depth conditions, hydrodynamics characteristics and port accessibility. The strong agreement between modeled high suitability zones and existing cage locations confirms the reliability of the proposed approach. Overall, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of integrating geomatics and remote sensing with MCDA as a decision support tool for sustainable mariculture planning, contributing to national food security, blue economy initiatives and environmentally responsible aquaculture development in Egypt.

detail.abstract: When dominant sellers possess substantial pricing power, buyer consolidation can serve as a countervailing force. We study this force using the 2012 merger of Express Scripts and Medco, the two largest U.S. pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) at the time. Exploiting geographic variation in exposure to the merger, we estimate the effects of a sharp increase in buyer concentration. Prices paid to pharmacies by health insurers for branded drugs fell by about 4% in highly exposed states, with effects lasting over two years and strongest in more competitive drug-product markets. Increased buyer power also weakened seller collusion: price increases during a subsequent generic drug cartel were significantly muted in states highly exposed to the PBM merger. However, the merger also generated distortions along the supply chain. Following reductions in reimbursements, pharmacies responded by dispensing smaller package sizes, a mechanical strategy that increases revenue through more frequent refills. This response raised patients' out-of-pocket costs, reduced medication adherence, and resulted in subsequent increases in emergency room visits for the same patients, associated with an estimated $208 to $623 million in additional annual healthcare costs. Overall, our results highlight a new competitive friction: buyer consolidation can discipline powerful sellers, but in multi-layer supply chains it can also distort intermediary behavior in ways that ultimately harm consumers.

title: Interchange Fees When Card Networks Compete for Card-issuing Bank

detail.title: Interchange Fees When Card Networks Compete for Card-issuing Bank
detail.abstract: Major credit card networks compete for attracting banks to distribute their credit card brand to consumers. They do not compete directly on consumers. This key characteristic is missing from most of the literature which views interchange fees as a mechanism for balancing between the number of merchants accepting cards and the number of credit card users. I develop a model where competing credit card networks set their interchange fees (paid by merchants to the card-issuing banks) to attract imperfectly-competitive profit-making banks to issue their card brand. Market failure occurs because each card network sets an excessively-high interchange fee to induce banks to issue more of its own card brand relative to the competing card brand.

detail.title: Synchronization of Poly-Crisis: Internal Contradictions in U.S.-China Relations and the Structural Inevitability of a Two-Front War in Northeast Asia (A 2026 Scenario Analysis)
detail.abstract:
This study analyzes the structural security risks emerging during the hypothesized transition of the international order in 2026, as the global system shifts from post Cold-War unipolarity toward a condition of intensified anarchy. Departing from traditional Power Transition Theory, which prioritizes relative material capabilities, this paper employs a scenario-based modeling approach to examine the interaction of three independent variables: (1) the erosion of U.S. deterrence resulting from domestic governance paralysis, (2) the strategic synchronization of revisionist actors (China, Russia, and North Korea), and (3) the strategic realignment of a key ally within the alliance network. 
The paper posits a hypothetical scenario involving a January 2026 federal state confrontation in the United States (the "Minneapolis Incident," drawing parallels to historical precedents such as the 2020 civil unrest and the 2021 Capitol events) and an accompanying fiscal cliff. It argues that these variables critically diminish U.S. power-projection capacity. When these conditions intersect with China's "gambling for resurrection" strategy amid structural economic deceleration, the outbreak of a multi-front conflict in Northeast Asia approaches a game-theoretic equilibrium. The study also considers counter-scenarios where U.S. institutional resilience or Chinese internal constraints mitigate these risks. It concludes that a shift in South Korea's strategic orientation could function as the decisive trigger collapsing regional deterrence, proposing systemic policy implications for managing compounded security failures.

detail.abstract: This article analyzes the relationship between public-led innovation and the dynamics of the Solow residual in Colombia over the last thirty years, incorporating a dimension typically absent from growth studies: the lack of motivation associated with personal, philosophical, and existential factors that influence how individuals perceive progress and life projects. From a growth theory perspective, the Solow residual reflects technological and efficiency changes not explained by the accumulation of capital and labor. It argues that public innovation policies, by impacting education, institutional quality, territorial planning, and social protection, indirectly influence this residual through their effect on motivation, agency, and future expectations.

title: Reimagining Agile Development With Psychology, GenAI and Neurodiversity In Mind for the Fifth Industrial Revolution

detail.title: Reimagining Agile Development With Psychology, GenAI and Neurodiversity In Mind for the Fifth Industrial Revolution
detail.abstract:
As smaller organisations enter the Fifth Industrial Revolution, agile development frameworks face growing pressure to support both rapid technological change and the cognitive realities of human contributors. Traditional methodologies such as Scrum and Kanban were developed under assumptions that prioritise speed, minimal documentation, and tolerance for ambiguity, assumptions that increasingly conflict with neurodiverse team compositions and the widespread integration of generative artificial intelligence. 

This white paper is intended as a practitioner-led contribution to organisational research and introduces Customer Centric Reinvention (CCR), a neuroinclusive project development framework designed to address the psychological, cognitive, and ethical limitations of contemporary agile practice. Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory alongside qualitative practitioner research, internal project observation, lived experience accounts, and targeted literature, the study identifies recurring accessibility challenges within agile environments, particularly for dyslexic contributors. 

CCR reframes agility through structured information architecture, predictable task sequencing, and persistent documentation, reducing cognitive load without sacrificing adaptability. The framework also formalises the role of artificial intelligence as a bounded, assistive tool for data-heavy tasks, while preserving human-led judgement, creativity, and narrative coherence. CCR is positioned as an evolution of agile practice, aligned with the human-centred priorities of the Fifth Industrial Revolution.

title: The Inclusion-Risk Paradox in FinTech and InsurTech: Effects of Algorithmic Access Expansion, Opacity, and Regulatory Safeguards

detail.title: The Inclusion-Risk Paradox in FinTech and InsurTech: Effects of Algorithmic Access Expansion, Opacity, and Regulatory Safeguards
detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of FinTech and InsurTech has reconfigured the delivery of financial and insurance services through algorithmic decision systems that simultaneously expand access and introduce new forms of institutional risk. While prior studies largely examine financial inclusion or risk in isolation, limited empirical work has investigated their coexistence within a single analytical framework. This study addresses this gap by examining the inclusion-risk paradox in FinTech and InsurTech systems, focusing on the effects of algorithmic access expansion, algorithmic opacity, and regulatory safeguards on financial and insurance inclusion and institutional vulnerability. Anchored in institutional theory and algorithmic governance perspectives, the study employs a quantitative, survey-based research design using data collected from senior banking executives, FinTech leaders, and InsurTech decision-makers in regulated financial institutions in the Philippines. Structural equation modeling is applied to test direct and moderating relationships, with rigorous validity and reliability assessments conducted to ensure measurement robustness. The results indicate that algorithmic access expansion significantly enhances financial and insurance inclusion, while algorithmic opacity increases institutional vulnerability. Regulatory safeguards are found to play a critical moderating role by strengthening inclusion outcomes and attenuating risk amplification. These findings empirically validate the inclusion-risk paradox and contribute to the literature by integrating inclusion and institutional vulnerability within a unified model. The study offers policy-relevant insights for regulators and industry leaders seeking to balance innovation-driven inclusion with institutional resilience in AI-enabled financial systems.

detail.abstract: The rapid pace of technological change continues to represent the principal challenge for modern competition policy. While the emergence of digital platforms and ecosystems has been invoked to justify a departure from traditional antitrust enforcement and has underpinned the recent wave of regulatory interventions, the rise of AI is reshaping the competitive landscape once again, calling into question the adequacy of existing analytical approaches and regulatory tools. Against this backdrop, by examining the expansion and role of AI-enabled assistants and agents, this paper seeks to provide a competition policy analysis of strategies aimed at integrating AI applications. It argues that the transformative and disruptive potential of AI technologies calls for a context-sensitive approach, rather than a mechanical and uncritical replication of the Big Tech-centric narrative that has characterized the recent competition policy in digital markets.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether industry classifications affect how firms select peers for executive compensation benchmarking. For identification, we exploit the setting of Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) reclassifications. We find that firms are significantly more likely to include peers whose GICS codes converge with their own and to drop peers whose codes diverge, with stronger effects when proxy advisors and passive investors provide greater oversight. We find no evidence of strategic selection, which suggests that these patterns reflect an update of the underlying benchmark. However, because reclassifications occur with a lag, compensation contracts may remain temporarily misaligned with evolving economic conditions. Overall, the results point to the influence of third-party classification providers in shaping corporate governance.

detail.abstract: We study residential segregation and access to public services across 1.5 million urban and rural neighborhoods in India. Nearly all regressive allocation is across neighborhoods within cities-at the most informal and least studied form of government. These inequalities are not visible in the aggregate data typically used for research and policy.

title: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Managing Perishable Healthcare Inventories under Sparse Demand
affiliations: Dalhousie University and Dalhousie University, Faculty of Engineering

detail.title: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Managing Perishable Healthcare Inventories under Sparse Demand
detail.abstract: Perishable healthcare inventories become especially difficult to manage when demand is intermittent, sparse, and poorly captured by classical stochastic models. Low-Titer O Whole Blood (LTOWB), a short-shelf-life trauma product currently under evaluation for civilian use in Canada, exemplifies this challenge: demand is highly zero-inflated, shortages carry severe clinical risk, and wastage represents the loss of a scarce donor resource. This study develops and evaluates learning-based control policies for LTOWB by formulating the replenishment problem as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process with age-structured inventory dynamics and Zero-Inflated Poisson (ZIP) demand. Exact stochastic dynamic programming (SDP) provides an optimal benchmark but becomes computationally infeasible as capacity or shelf life increases. To address this limitation, we compare two reinforcement-learning paradigms: model-based Approximate Dynamic Programming (ADP), which exploits the known transition structure, and model-free Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which learns solely from simulated experience. Using GPU-accelerated SDP to obtain optimal solutions for small instances, we evaluate both methods across 16 demand regimes ranging from extreme sparsity to moderate utilization. ADP produces policies statistically indistinguishable from the SDP benchmark in all regimes while remaining computationally efficient. PPO achieves comparable performance only when demand provides sufficient information density and requires orders of magnitude more simulated experience, equivalent to more than 18,000 years of hospital operations, to overcome reward sparsity. A scalability analysis identifies the operational thresholds at which exact SDP becomes infeasible and ADP emerges as the practical surrogate. These findings indicate systematic performance differences between model-based and model-free learning under zero-inflated demand.

title: Designing the Invisible Hand: Managing Gig Worker Behavior through Digital Influence

detail.title: Designing the Invisible Hand: Managing Gig Worker Behavior through Digital Influence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that there is no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper.

detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Online gig platforms rely on loosely monitored workers whose service quality varies substantially. Since platforms cannot fully mandate behavior, workers often learn social norms from online communities. We study whether platforms should actively shape these norms by deploying "online brigades", defined as coordinated influence campaigns designed to shift perceived best practices. We analyze the operational viability of this strategy and its interaction with commission design. 

Methodology/results: We develop a game-theoretic model in which heterogeneous workers trade off their intrinsic ideals against peer pressure. Our analysis reveals that digital influence is a double-edged sword. While moderate influence can align worker behavior and increase demand, excessive influence induces overshooting, whereby worker behavior shifts beyond customer preferences and decreases demand. Furthermore, shifting norms is costly. We find that platforms typically have to lower commission rates to compensate workers for deviating from their ideals. Consequently, deploying an online brigade is profitable only when realized influence is moderate and market potential is sufficiently high, and it becomes less attractive as workforce heterogeneity increases. 

Managerial implications: Our findings caution managers against viewing online influence solely as a demand-enhancing tool. Although influence campaigns can raise demand, they may simultaneously compress margins through lower optimal commissions. Effective deployment therefore requires joint consideration of influence intensity, pricing, and workforce composition. Platforms must assess both the alignment gap between workers and customers and the degree of workforce heterogeneity to avoid the financial and behavioral risks of miscalibrated influence.

detail.abstract: We study Weighted Mean Correlation (WMC): the implied equi-correlation parameter that matches the portfolio quadratic form (w^T C w ) for a given weight vector (w). Equivalently, WMC is the single off-diagonal correlation that reproduces the portfolio’s correlation-risk contribution under an equi-correlation approximation. Our contribution is algebraic and computational. We present two equivalent closed forms—(i) a polarization identity in correlation space and (ii) a raw-returns variance identity—that enable exact streaming computation in O(NT) time and O(T) memory, avoiding pairwise loops and N×N storage. We treat missing observations exactly via weighted and unweighted pair–day identities (with optional time weights), and derive incremental add/remove updates and a first-order weight calculus that support constrained “what-if” edits. Estimator-consistent day/name/group decompositions enable attribution and “what changed” diagnostics. We also summarize practical estimation conventions (EWMA, shrinkage, robust scaling), bounds and edge cases, and verification checks.

detail.abstract: The past three decades have witnessed a dramatic expansion of artisanal and smallscale gold mining (ASgM), transforming the economic and spatial opportunities of tens of millions of people. We show how this transformation has shaped urbanization in Sub-Saharan Africa since 1975. Our empirical strategy exploits plausibly exogenous variation in ASgM activity driven by the interaction between international gold-price shocks and local geological suitability for artisanal extraction, and combines it with new continent-wide data on urban population, nighttime lights, and household welfare. Although ASgM is commonly viewed as a rural activity, we find that ASgM exposure significantly accelerates urbanization, accounting for roughly five percent of total urban population growth. This expansion takes the form of extensive, decentralized urbanization: new towns emerge in remote, infrastructure-poor areas, while the growth of pre-existing towns and cities does not accelerate. Both new and existing urban entities exposed to ASgM exhibit lower living standards and limited industrial activity. Overall, ASgM contributes to a fragmented pattern of urbanization without structural transformation.

detail.abstract: Intrinsic motivation is highly valued in the workplace, with employees encouraged to express the meaning and enjoyment they derive from their work. However, the current research identifies a cost of intrinsic motivation: managers allocate additional tasks to employees they perceive as more (vs. less) intrinsically motivated. We establish this effect across task allocation paradigms using managers' actual employees, profiles of real workers randomly assigned to managers, and a lab experiment with a salient financial downside for the chosen employee (Studies 1a, 1b, and 2). Managers' preference to allocate additional tasks to intrinsically motivated employees is serially mediated by the naïve belief that these employees will enjoy the additional task (i.e., motive oversimplification), which in turn reduces perceived risk of burnout from the additional work (Study 2; Supplemental Studies 2 and 3). Notably, this preference persists in a six-day longitudinal study with repeated allocation decisions (Study 3) and can negatively affect organizations (Study 3 post-test). Two theory-driven interventions attenuate this preference by intervening on managers' decision environment (Study 4) and beliefs (Study 5). This research advances theory on motivation, person perception, and task allocation decisions, and offers insights and solutions for the paradoxical burnout experienced by individuals who derive joy from their work.

title: Digital Transformation in Airline Logistics: Enhancing Operational Efficiency through AI-Driven Predictive Analytics and Blockchain Integration

detail.title: Digital Transformation in Airline Logistics: Enhancing Operational Efficiency through AI-Driven Predictive Analytics and Blockchain Integration
detail.abstract: This study aims to develop and validate a Predictive AI-Based Supply Chain Visibility Framework (PASCVF) tailored for airline logistics management. Employing a mixed-methods approach within a Design Science Research framework, the research integrates advanced digital technologies including IoT, RFID, blockchain, and AI-driven predictive analytics to enhance operational transparency, reduce lead times, and optimize inventory management. Data were collected from major international airlines using structured interviews, operational records, and simulation modeling. The results reveal significant improvements, including a 20% reduction in lead time, a 25% decrease in stock-out frequency, and a 5-10% reduction in Cost per Available Seat Kilometer (CASK). These findings provide empirical support for the framework, offering actionable insights for enhancing strategic decision-making and operational resilience in the aviation industry. The study contributes to academic theory by extending digital transformation models and has practical implications, recommending that airline executives invest in integrated digital solutions to achieve sustainable performance gains.

detail.abstract: This book is perhaps the first comprehensive, research-backed attempt to analyze India’s economic journey in depth. It identifies key structural impediments and proposes actionable policy solutions. Aimed at policymakers, economists, academics, and informed readers, the book bridges crucial knowledge gaps and advocates for strategic reforms often unconventional and based on out-of-the-box thinking to help India realize its aspiration of becoming a robust economy and a global economic powerhouse. India, currently the world’s fifth-largest economy by nominal GDP and third largest by purchasing power parity (PPP), has a diverse economic structure comprising agriculture, industry, and a dominant services sector. Since gaining independence in 1947, India has transitioned from a mixed economy to a more liberalized one, especially after the 1991 economic reforms that opened the country to global trade and investment. Agriculture still employs over 40% of the workforce but contributes only 16–18% to GDP, reflecting persistent structural challenges. Industry and manufacturing account for about 25–30% of GDP, buoyed by initiatives like "Make in India," while the services sector—led by IT, finance, and telecommunications— drives more than 50% of the economy. Despite impressive GDP growth, India continues to face several enduring challenges, including infrastructure deficits, high unemployment, complex regulatory frameworks, corruption, and regional disparities in education and development. These persistent issues hinder the full impact of developmental efforts, particularly at the grassroots level. This research-based book delves deeply into each of these challenges and proposes bold, sometimes radical, solutions to overcome them. Many of the issues, the book argues, are solvable with the right policies and governance, which could significantly accelerate the country’s development trajectory. This book will prove invaluable for policymakers, aspirants preparing for competitive examinations, management institutions, and anyone interested in understanding the complexities and opportunities of the Indian economic landscape.

title: Trade Credit as an Endogenous Asset: Data-Driven Admission and Non-Bank Financial Intermediation in Supply Chains

detail.title: Trade Credit as an Endogenous Asset: Data-Driven Admission and Non-Bank Financial Intermediation in Supply Chains
detail.abstract: This study proposes a conceptual mechanism to explain how credit is endogenously generated and transformed within supply chains prior to formal financial intermediation. Existing literature on digital finance and shadow banking has largely focused on financial instruments or information frictions, while paying insufficient attention to the origin and translation of credit itself. This paper argues that supply chains generate endogenous trade credit through repeated transactions and fulfillment structures, that digitalization enhances the verifiability and transferability of this credit without creating it, and that non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) govern the admission of such credit into the financial system before its amplification by commercial banks. Rather than treating digital finance as a process of financial innovation, this paper conceptualizes it as a mechanism of credit translation. In this framework, data function as carriers that render trade credit auditable and transferable, NBFIs operate as gatekeepers that determine which credits become financeable, and banks act as dependent amplifiers that leverage already verified and structured claims. The model establishes a causal sequence from real economic transactions to financial amplification, clarifying the structural origins of liquidity risk and hidden leverage within supply-chainbased intermediation.

detail.abstract: We present a thermodynamic framework for modelling value capture in markets where customers require a threshold level of coverage before a transaction succeeds. Customers value not so much the outcome of the individual touchpoint but the overall experience. Our main focus is on Radio Access Network Optimisation (RAN), but we will use a jargon-free example from Public Mass Transport as a motivation. While entropy and information measures have been used as heuristics in optimisation and search (e.g., entropy search in Bayesian optimisation and entropy-guided exploration in reinforcement learning) , the present work defines entropy as a state-level measure of uncertainty in threshold satisfaction outcomes and integrates it with free energy bounds to guide breadth-first action selection under budget constraints in infrastructure planning. This combination is novel and captures the practical objective of maximising realised value rather than information about an unobserved optimum.

detail.title: P-MACTR Matrix: A Reality-Weighted Market Evaluation Framework for Modern Industries
detail.abstract: Traditional portfolio analysis tools such as the BCG Matrix and the GE–McKinsey Matrix rely on simplified assumptions about market growth and market share. While effective in stable industrial eras, these frameworks fail to capture the complexity of modern economies characterized by aggressive competition, regulatory uncertainty, technological disruption, and accounting-driven profitability. This paper proposes a new analytical framework—the P-MACTR Matrix™—which evaluates firms and products using seven reality-weighted dimensions: Profitability Reality, Market Share, Market Growth, Cash Flow Strength, Competition Intensity, Technology Position, and Regulation Impact. The framework introduces a Profit Reality Filter (PRF) to distinguish real, sustainable profits from accounting or short-term profits. The P-MACTR Matrix provides a more accurate, future-oriented, and risk-adjusted tool for investors, strategists, policymakers, and entrepreneurs.

title: Prompting in the Wild: A Qualitative Taxonomy of Practitioner-Driven Prompt Engineering Methods
affiliations: CirroLytix Research Services

detail.title: Prompting in the Wild: A Qualitative Taxonomy of Practitioner-Driven Prompt Engineering Methods
detail.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly embedded in professional and everyday workflows, prompt engineering has emerged as a critical yet loosely defined skill. While formal prompt engineering frameworks have proliferated in recent years, much of the existing literature emphasizes idealized prompt structures, benchmarks, and synthetic tasks, offering limited insight into how prompting is practiced in real-world settings. This paper addresses this gap by examining prompting strategies as they emerge organically among practitioners. Drawing on practitioner-generated comments from a public social media discussion soliciting prompting methodologies, this study employs qualitative thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns in real-world prompting behavior. The analysis reveals a diverse set of prompting strategies that cluster into several categories, including context-first and living context management, role and persona assignment, structural and formatting control, meta-cognitive prompting, iterative conversational workflows, verification and skepticism mechanisms, and affective, social, and linguistic strategies. The primary contribution of this work is a practice-based taxonomy of prompting strategies "in the wild," highlighting forms of interaction that extend beyond formal prompt engineering models. In particular, the findings underscore the importance of social framing, conversational iteration, and meta-strategic collaboration between users and AI systems. The paper concludes by discussing implications for practitioners seeking more effective prompting workflows, for tool designers developing interfaces and infrastructure to support real-world use, and for researchers aiming to bridge formal prompt engineering research with practitioner knowledge.

title: Relational Integrity in AI: Preserving Human Agency, Accountability, and Meaning Under Pressure

detail.title: Relational Integrity in AI: Preserving Human Agency, Accountability, and Meaning Under Pressure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: As AI systems increasingly operate in language-mediated and relational contexts, many of the risks they introduce do not arise from discrete failures, misuse, or malicious intent. Instead, harm often emerges through gradual shifts in how systems are interpreted, relied upon, and positioned within human judgment and institutional practice. These shifts are frequently well-intended, incentive-aligned, and normalized through ordinary use, allowing role clarity, accountability, and relational boundaries to erode even when systems appear effective. The Relational Integrity in AI Framework (RIAF) offers a diagnostic approach to these dynamics. Rather than treating relational harm as a matter of compliance, output control, or user error, RIAF conceptualizes it as a structural phenomenon shaped by cumulative interaction, interpretive signals, and institutional embedding. The framework introduces relational drift as a precursor to stabilized structural failure, identifies a canonical set of relational integrity failure modes, and argues that sustained protection depends on preserving specific human capacities rather than enforcing static rules or prescriptions. RIAF is not an implementation guide or ethical checklist. It is a conditioning framework designed to support reflection, pressure-testing of relational integrity, and responsible judgment in contexts where AI systems increasingly mediate meaning, authority, care, and decision-making.

title: Mixed Methods Designs

detail.title: Mixed Methods Designs
detail.abstract: Mixed-method research has gained popularity as one of the most recent developments in research methodologies and approaches to combining quantitative and qualitative research. To better comprehend our research problem and answer our research question, we can use both qualitative and quantitative data. We can develop "a complex" picture of social phenomena by assessing both the outcomes of the research in terms of numeracy (i.e., quantitative) and the process (i.e., qualitative) (Greene & Caracelli, 1997, p. 7) [1]. The current chapter is divided into the following sections: Section I provided an overview of "What is Mixed-Methods Research?" while Section II detailed the historical development of mixedmethods research. Section III addresses "Why and When to Use Mixed Methods Research." Section IV gives a concise summary of the various dimensions of a mixed-methods study design in relation to contemporary sinereos. The fifth section, "Ethical Issues in Mixed Methods Research," has been accomplished. The steps involved in conducting mixed-methods research were outlined in Section VI. Finally, in Section VII, I have discussed some concluding remarks.

title: Labour Market Power and Automation

detail.title: Labour Market Power and Automation
detail.abstract: I show novel evidence using French administrative data that automation reduced wage markdowns by 3%-reflecting increased labour market power-and increased concentration by 20%, with effects intensifying over time. To quantify the aggregate implications, I develop a general equilibrium model with oligopsonistic labour markets, endogenous automation adoption, and firm entry. Using the reducedform evidence to discipline the model, I find that median welfare would be approximately 13% higher, and aggregate output 2% higher, had automation occurred without raising labour market power.

title: Programmable Fiscal Instruments for Welfare Delivery: The Case for Annapurna Coin and a Welfare Digital Public Infrastructure in India

detail.title: Programmable Fiscal Instruments for Welfare Delivery: The Case for Annapurna Coin and a Welfare Digital Public Infrastructure in India
detail.abstract:
India’s welfare architecture has been significantly reshaped over the last decade through digitisation, Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT), and national digital rails such as Aadhaar and the Public Financial Management System (PFMS). These reforms have improved transfer-stage efficiency and reduced diversion at disbursement. However, persistent challenges remain in welfare schemes where policy objectives are outcome-specific, particularly in food security and nutrition. Cash transfers are fully fungible and sensitive to price variation, while in-kind delivery remains administratively rigid and vulnerable to leakage, creating a structural trade-off between efficiency and outcome assurance.

This paper introduces programmable fiscal instruments as a distinct class of budget-issued welfare instruments designed to address this gap. Unlike cash transfers, vouchers, or digital currency, programmable fiscal instruments embed purpose, usage constraints, and settlement rules directly within the instrument, enabling outcome-specific welfare delivery without monetary or central-bank balance-sheet implications. The paper situates this concept within a Welfare Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) framework and argues that instrument design constitutes a missing architectural layer in contemporary welfare systems.

The paper examines Annapurna Coin and Milk Coin as concrete instantiations of this framework. Annapurna Coin illustrates a population-scale instrument for staple food security, while Milk Coin demonstrates targeted nutrition support for specific demographic groups. Through architectural, legal, and economic analysis, the paper shows how programmable fiscal instruments preserve beneficiary choice while enforcing purpose constraints, support multi-vendor participation, and generate policy-relevant utilisation data. The paper reframes welfare reform as a problem of fiscal instrument design rather than transfer modality.

title: Ogoni-Ibibio Intergroup Relations Since the Pre-colonial Era to 2023.
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Ogoni-Ibibio Intergroup Relations Since the Pre-colonial Era to 2023.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract:
Abstract

The intergroup relationship between the Ogoni and Ibibio communities has been a prominent aspect of Southern Nigerian history since the pre-colonial era. This research aims to explore the dynamics, interactions, and transformations that have shaped this relationship over time. By examining various historical sources, including oral traditions, archival records, and scholarly works, this study seeks to provide a comprehensive analysis of the intergroup dynamics between the Ogoni and Ibibio peoples.  The research will delve into the pre-colonial era, a period characterized by cultural exchanges, trade relationships, and occasional conflicts between the Ogoni and Ibibio communities. It will investigate the socio-economic, political, and cultural factors that influenced their interactions during this period, shedding light on the nature of their relationship. 

Furthermore, this research will also examine the impact of the colonial era on the intergroup relationship. The arrival of European powers and subsequent colonization brought about significant changes, including the introduction of a new administrative structure, economic transformations, and the imposition of colonial policies. These factors had a profound effect on the Ogoni-Ibibio relationship, altering power dynamics, trade patterns, and cultural practices. 

The post-colonial era will also be explored to understand how the intergroup relationship has evolved in the wake of Nigeria's independence. This period witnessed the rise of nationalism, ethnic tensions, and political struggles, which further influenced the dynamics between the Ogoni and Ibibio communities. The research will delve into these aspects, analyzing the role of nationalism and social movements in shaping their relationship. 

Through this research, a comprehensive understanding of the intergroup relationship between the Ogoni and Ibibio communities will be achieved. The findings will contribute to existing knowledge and provide insights into the historical and contemporary dynamics that have influenced their interactions. This study aims to foster a deeper appreciation of the complex intergroup relationships that have shaped Nigerian history, with the hope of promoting better understanding and harmony among these communities in the present and future.

title:

A Rigorous Mathematical Framework for Earth's Celestial Dynamics and its Multi-Site Empirical Validation Across Ancient Global Observatories

detail.title:
A Cosmic Dance: The Unified Principle 
A Rigorous Mathematical Framework for Earth's Celestial Dynamics and its Multi-Site Empirical Validation Across Ancient Global Observatories
detail.abstract: This paper introduces The Unified Principle, a mathematical and empirical framework that defines Earth's fundamental rotational and orbital constants. It establishes a 364-day Unified Year (TY) and a 6.5-day Unified Day (TD), yielding exactly 56 rotations per year (NR), alongside a constant 23.5° axial tilt (α). The paper details hierarchical timekeeping, extending to Unified Hours and Minutes, and demonstrates the global, observable validation of these constants via ancient observatories, including Stonehenge (England), Serpent Mound (North America), the Pyramids of Giza (Egypt), Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple (India), and Chankillo (Peru). The study provides a consistent, empirically verifiable model of Earth's motion, lunar phases, eclipses, and celestial calibration, offering precise evidence for a spherical Earth while illustrating the sophistication of ancient astronomers' observational practices.

title: What Do Alif-Lam-Mim Actually Do? Rethinking the Disconnected Letters as Structural Thresholds in the Quran

detail.title: What Do Alif-Lam-Mim Actually Do? Rethinking the Disconnected Letters as Structural Thresholds in the Quran
