detail.abstract: Hurūf al-Muqaṭṭaʿāt: A Structural-Functional Reading of the Disconnected Letters in the Quran The disconnected letters (ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿāt)—letter combinations such as Alif-Lam-Mim and Ha Mim appearing at the beginning of twenty-nine Quranic suras—have constituted one of Islamic scholarship’s most enduring interpretive challenges. Classical authorities adopted tafwīḍ (entrusting their meaning to God alone), while modern interpreters pursue numerological solutions. Despite fourteen centuries of inquiry, no consensus exists regarding what these letters mean. This monograph proposes a methodological reorientation: instead of asking “What do these letters mean?” it investigates “What do these letters do?” Drawing on reader-response theory, cognitive psychology, and textual analysis, this study argues that the disconnected letters function as structural thresholds—markers calibrating readers’ cognitive and epistemic positioning at sura openings. Through systematic examination of placement, distribution, and textual correlation, the study demonstrates three key findings: (1) their selective distribution reflects functional deployment—suras lacking them employ alternative threshold mechanisms (praise formulas, oaths, imperatives); (2) different letter groups correlate with distinct discourse types (Alif-Lam-Mim with pedagogical content, Ha-Mim with polemical defense, Alif-Lam-Ra with prophetic narratives); (3) they operate simultaneously as cognitive disruptors, acoustic attention-markers, and reader-activation devices. This functional interpretation accounts for features semantic approaches cannot explain while respecting classical epistemic humility. By analyzing observable patterns rather than decoding hidden meanings, the study reveals how textual elements achieve significance through function rather than semantic content.

title: New Evidence on State-Dependent Fiscal Multipliers
affiliations: Bank of Italy

detail.title: New Evidence on State-Dependent Fiscal Multipliers

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1512
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Building on the dataset and identification strategy of Ramey and Zubairy (2018), this paper investigates the dynamic effects of fiscal shocks using a state-dependent local projection approach. By interacting fiscal shocks with a continuous state variable, the analysis captures how fiscal multipliers evolve over the business cycle. This approach is novel within this literature, as most previous studies rely on two-regime estimates to account for non-linearity. The results indicate that the government spending multiplier varies significantly, ranging from near zero during expansions to slightly below one in downturns. While this evidence highlights meaningful state dependence in the transmission of fiscal policy, the relatively modest size of the estimated multipliers calls for caution in drawing strong conclusions about the effectiveness of countercyclical policies.

title: Energy Shocks
affiliations: University of London

detail.title: Energy Shocks
detail.abstract: The paper incorporates endogenous energy sector composed of coal, gas and oil in a Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) model and estimates using Bayesian methodology, providing evidence that energy shocks are the main contributor to the latest post-pandemic inflation episode and the variance of the monetary policy. The model augmented with financial frictions corrects counterfactual response of positive investment. An intriguing finding is that while the short run responses of output, consumption, and investment are negative but in the medium run swing to positive, not uncovered in any other relevant paper in literature. The substitution effect improves the productivity of capital and labor leading to positive medium term growth. Question is how policy makers can leverage these insights of positive dynamic response for transition towards a low-carbon economy? The paper also shows that well functioning financial markets can reduce the policy burden by stabilising the macro aggregates.

title: Heterogeneous Equity Market Responses to a Geopolitical Tariff Threat
affiliations: Middle Tennessee State University - Department of Economics and Finance

detail.title: Heterogeneous Equity Market Responses to a Geopolitical Tariff Threat
detail.abstract: This paper examines country-specific equity market responses to a politically conditioned tariff threat using the synthetic control method. The analysis focuses on the January 17, 2026 announcement in which the U.S. administration threatened escalating tariffs on imports from eight NATO countries unless an unrelated geopolitical demand-the purchase of Greenlandwas met. The policy was unusual in that tariffs were explicitly tied to a non-trade objective and selectively applied to close political and military allies of the United States. Using daily national equity market indices, the analysis reveals substantial heterogeneity in market responses to the same policy shock. All targeted countries exhibit negative post-announcement deviations from their synthetic benchmarks, except the United Kingdom.

title: Computational Foundations for Increasing Returns: Connecting the Milei-Reidel Framework to Turing-Walras-Chaitin

detail.title: Computational Foundations for Increasing Returns: Connecting the Milei-Reidel Framework to Turing-Walras-Chaitin
detail.abstract: Milei and Reidel (2026) demonstrate that increasing returns to scale (IRS) generate minimum viable scale constraints and poverty traps through a fold geometry in the steady-state feasibility set. Their central policy conclusion-that structural interventions fragmenting scale can be counterproductive-challenges standard presumptions about antitrust policy. This paper shows that the Turing-Walras-Chaitin (TWC) framework provides computational foundations for the Milei-Reidel result: IRS emerge naturally from the combinatorial structure of program space, and their insights about scale thresholds find formal expression in the dynamics of technological exploration. The TWC framework also provides a formal demonstration of Hayek's (1945) insight about the limits of planning: equilibrium in the limit economy is provably undecidable, meaning that optimal intervention cannot be computed by any algorithm. We establish a bridge between the two frameworks, showing that the minimum viable labor scale of IRS models corresponds to a minimum viable exploration scale in TWC, and that both capture the same fundamental insight: scale matters, and policy interventions that suppress it can trap economies in low-productivity regimes.

title: Memory Warriors, Pluralists and Abnegators in Constituional Interpretation: An Essay on Jack Balkin's Pluralist Originalism in Memory and Authority
affiliations: Boston University - School of Law and

detail.title: Memory Warriors, Pluralists and Abnegators in Constituional Interpretation: An Essay on Jack Balkin's Pluralist Originalism in Memory and Authority

publicationDetails.detailsText: Boston Univ. School of Law Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Boston University School of Law Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Jack Balkin’s Memory and Authority: The Uses of History in Constitutional Interpretation brings into conversation the scholarly insights of constitutional theory, history, and the growing field of “the politics of memory,” especially the concept of the “memory entrepreneur.”

Balkin appropriately connects the memory wars in American constitutional law back to Eastern European memory wars during the World Wars and their aftermath. Prompted by Balkin, we turn to Jan Kubik and Michael Bernhard edited volume Twenty Years After Communism (2014), which has become even more widely influential after Putin’s invasion of Ukraine and a new round of Eastern European memory wars. They propose four categories of memory entrepreneurs (“mnemonic actors”) in post-Soviet countries: “mnemonic warriors” who claim a single “true” interpretation of the past, opposed to all others who cultivate “wrong” or “false” interpretations; “mnemonic pluralists” who embrace multiple narratives and traditions; “mnemonic abnegators” who deny the significance of the past in favor of the present; and “mnemonic prospectives” who have a faith in an inevitable future (e.g., utopian Marxist historical materialists).

We suggest this taxonomy may be a helpful guide for American constitutional politics. The “memory pluralist” category is perhaps the majority of American constitutional law professors, maybe even a plurality of the U.S. Supreme Court and the federal and state bench, who do not give exclusive weight to history, but still give substantial weight to history (e.g., Philip Bobbit’s modalities, Balkin’s “living originalism” and his “thin originalism.”).

Some “thick originalists” are more “Memory Anti-Pluralists” than “Warriors.” We reserve the category of “Memory Warrior” for those constitutional interpreters who are consciously fighting for an exclusive, comprehensive national narrative of us vs. them. These warriors include ideological originalists (especially the ones who seem to rely on a general narrative arc rather than specific historical evidence), but they also may include the “history-and-tradition” conservatives, common-good constitutionalists, and perhaps some progressive-left memory warriors who have a more exclusive interpretation of past events than pluralists do.

Balkin rightly criticizes originalism for its “memory entrepreneurialism” that narrows the field of who “counts” and who is excluded, exacerbating constitutional law’s democratic deficit. We think the “memory warrior” category helps sort out the more problematic approaches, and we suggest a solution: a high burden of proof about consensus and public meaning to mitigate this democratic deficit, to reduce judicial legitimacy problems, and to slow down “warrior” judicial activism.

title: Financial Agents Know Everything: The FAKE Ground of Modern Macroeconomic Models

detail.title: Financial Agents Know Everything: The FAKE Ground of Modern Macroeconomic Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests related to this work.

detail.abstract:
Modern macroeconomic models rely on expectations to close dynamic systems and generate equilibrium predictions. These expectations are typically justified through rational expectations or related learning frameworks, yet the epistemic conditions required for such justifications are rarely examined explicitly. This paper argues that, for macroeconomic purposes, these conditions amount to an implicit assumption that financial agents possess functionally omniscient knowledge of the economic environment. To form model-consistent expectations, agents must know the correct structural model, the stochastic processes governing exogenous variables, the laws of motion of endogenous states, the equilibrium mappings linking beliefs to outcomes, and the policy regimes shaping future dynamics. Although models do not assume literal omniscience, these informational requirements are sufficient to generate behavior indistinguishable from that of an omniscient agent with respect to macroeconomic decision-making.

The paper introduces the concept of functional omniscience to distinguish this epistemic requirement from assumptions about perfect rationality, cognitive ability, or psychological realism. It shows how functional omniscience enters macroeconomic models mechanically through rational-expectations closure, persists in learning-based extensions, and underwrites representative-agent constructions. When this assumption is relaxed, homogeneous beliefs and representative expectations lose their epistemic justification, and heterogeneity in beliefs and behavior emerges as a structural consequence rather than a modeling choice. FAKE is used as a diagnostic label for an implicit epistemic ground, not as a critique of economists or a claim of methodological error.

title: The Unified Principle: A Unified Celestial Framework and Its Empirical Validation for a Spherical Earth
affiliations: Founder, Unified Principle

detail.title: The Unified Principle: A Unified Celestial Framework and Its Empirical Validation for a Spherical Earth
detail.abstract: This paper presents The Unified Principle (UP), a self-consistent mathematical model of celestial mechanics defined by an Earth orbital period of precisely 364 days () and an Earth rotational period of exactly 6.5 days (). This exact integer relationship yields rotations per orbital cycle, ensuring an intrinsically non-drifting celestial calendar. The principle posits a constant Earth axial tilt of () and describes the Moon's orbit as a consistent helical trajectory relative to the Sun, completing a 28-day synodic cycle. Calibrated to the June 20, 2025 Summer Solstice as Unified Day 1 of Unified Year 1, the principle projects predictable events over a 10-year span. Observations of solar and lunar phenomena at geographically distinct ancient structures-Stonehenge (51.18° N), Giza Pyramids (29.98° N), Brihadisvara Temple (10.78° N), and Machu Picchu (13.16° S)-provide empirical validation for a spherical Earth, derived entirely from the internal mathematical framework of the Unified Principle.

title: Foundations of Algorithmic Economics: A TuringWalrasChaitin Framework Part II: Static Equilibrium Theory

detail.title: Foundations of Algorithmic Economics: A TuringWalrasChaitin Framework Part II: Static Equilibrium Theory
detail.abstract: This paper develops the static equilibrium theory for the TuringWalrasChaitin framework. Taking the technological frontier Ω n as given, we formalize the optimization problems of rms and consumers, state the conditions for Walrasian equilibrium with Cobb-Douglas preferences, and establish existence and local stability. We prove four main results: (1) for any nite technological frontier, a competitive equilibrium exists; (2) under gross substitutes, the tâtonnement process converges; (3) the equilibrium is computable in nite time; (4) in the limit as the technological frontier expands to include all halting programs, the equilibrium problem becomes algorithmically undecidable. This nal result is proven via explicit reduction to the halting problem and constitutes the paper's main contribution.

title: Techno-Economic Assessment of a 500 MW Offshore Wind Farm at Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh
affiliations: and

detail.title: Techno-Economic Assessment of a 500 MW Offshore Wind Farm at Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh
detail.abstract: The rising electricity demand and decarbonization goals make offshore wind a practical path to energy security for Bangladesh. Yet country-specific, end-to-end studies that connect wind resource to investable economics are limited. This paper evaluates a 500 MW wind farm project of Cox’s Bazar using a transparent, reproducible resource to revenue workflow. ERA5 (2020–2024) wind data are vector combined at 100 m, extrapolated to 150 m and converted to turbine power with air density correction. The model consists of a layout of 42 turbines and considers a conservative, multiplicative loss stack. Techno-economics are calculated in HOMER software and cross checked with a discounted cash flow model reflecting relevant financing (10% nominal WACC, 2% indexation for tariff and O&M) for Bangladesh. The project delivers a net annual energy production of 1.48 TWh at a capacity factor of 33.4% and an engineering LCOE of $98/MWh. The first-year tariff $0.11/kWh, the base case delivers an NPV of $0.41B with a discounted payback in Year 13. Sensitivity results indicate bankability is dominated by WACC and CAPEX while O&M and the capacity factor have secondary influence. Relative to today’s grid, the project would avoid 0.94 Mt CO₂ annually. Overall, the offshore wind project studied here for Bangladesh appears feasible within a $0.10–$0.11/kWh PPA corridor provided policy measures reduce financing risk and support from local supply chains. The workflow and dataset are openly reproducible and can guide site screening and investment decisions in emerging offshore wind markets.

title: A Systems-based Framework for Embedding Generative AI in Financial Decision Systems

detail.title: A Systems-based Framework for Embedding Generative AI in Financial Decision Systems
detail.abstract:
The increasing adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in financial markets has
largely been driven by prompt-centric and model-focused experimentation. While such
approaches demonstrate localized capabilities, they frequently fail when confronted with
the structural requirements of financial systems, including auditability, regulatory
compliance, contextual stability, and accountability. This paper proposes a
comprehensive systems-based framework for embedding generative AI within financial
decision systems.
The framework conceptualizes AI models not as autonomous decision-makers but as
reasoning components embedded within structured, observable, and auditable workflows.
It explicitly separates deterministic computation, AI-driven inference, contextual memory
via retrieval-augmented systems, and human judgment, all operating under continuous
observability and governance. The framework is intentionally non-linear and iterative,
reflecting the reflexive nature of financial reasoning.
Through extended, operationally realistic scenarios spanning mutual fund research,
trading research, and risk management, this paper demonstrates how the framework
generalizes across financial domains. The paper further develops a taxonomy of failure
modes observed in practice, proposes a system-level evaluation lens for AI models, and
maps the framework to emerging regulatory requirements, particularly the European Union
Artificial Intelligence Act. The contribution of this paper is conceptual rather than
algorithmic, offering a durable mental model for applying AI in finance under uncertainty,
regulation, and accountability.

title: The Wynn Framework
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Wynn Framework
detail.abstract: Despite unprecedented access to information, human decision-making has become increasingly unstable. Individuals and institutions exhibit escalating conflict, defensive rigidity, and explanatory overload. These failures are commonly attributed to ignorance, moral deficiency, or incentive misalignment. This framework rejects those explanations. Human instability is not primarily a failure of intelligence, character, or motivation. It is a failure of coordination under uncertainty. Humans are biologically near-identical pattern-matching systems operating without reliable shared reference points. When decentralized agents lack signals that are both observable and known to be observable by others, coordination becomes underdetermined. In this condition, timing, intent, and meaning cannot reliably align. Ambiguity is resolved locally, narratives substitute for structure, and defensive stabilization becomes the system default. The Wynn Framework formalizes this failure mode. It treats human conflict as an engineering problem rather than a psychological or moral one, identifying the absence or degradation of common-knowledge coordination signals as the primary driver of misunderstanding across scales — from interpersonal conflict to institutional collapse. Trust, cooperation, and equilibrium are treated not as virtues to be cultivated, but as emergent properties of systems with sufficient coordination integrity. This work does not offer a universal theory of mind. It offers a structural diagnostic and repair architecture: a set of primitives and protocols designed to reduce interpretive load, restore shared reference, and convert defensive rigidity back into inquiry. Its validity is measured by a single criterion: Does it reduce misunderstanding without requiring persuasion, virtue, or belief?

title:
The Voynich Mandate: Section-by-Section Decipherment 
A Complete Unveiling of Universal Code
affiliations: Founder, Unified Principle

detail.title:
The Voynich Mandate: Section-by-Section Decipherment 
A Complete Unveiling of Universal Code
detail.abstract: The Voynich Manuscript has long been considered an indecipherable enigma, with centuries of cryptographic, linguistic, and historical inquiry yielding no consensus on its content or meaning. This manuscript introduces a systematic framework for interpreting the Voynich Manuscript through the lens of the Unified Principle, a universal method for identifying recurring patterns and structures across scales-from biological growth to cosmic mechanics. By treating each section of the manuscript as a precise repository of encoded directives, this study deciphers actionable instructions in four domains: botanical generation, astronomical alignment, fluid and biological systems, and cosmological architecture. The methodology combines fractal analysis, L-system modeling, orbital mechanics, network flow theory, and symmetry operations to map underlying mathematical principles encoded in the manuscript. While the literal language remains unknown, the structure, patterns, and algorithmic regularities reveal a sophisticated, universal system of design that can be applied across biology, cosmology, and physical systems. This work establishes a rigorous, verifiable approach to understanding the Voynich Manuscript's instructions, demonstrating that even in the absence of semantic clarity, its internal logic embodies a complete and actionable blueprint for universal order.

title: Foundations of Algorithmic Economics: A Turing-Walras-Chaitin Framework. Part III: Endogenous Technological Change and Supercomputational Growth

detail.title: Foundations of Algorithmic Economics: A Turing-Walras-Chaitin Framework. Part III: Endogenous Technological Change and Supercomputational Growth
detail.abstract: This paper develops the growth theory for the Turing-Walras-Chaitin framework. We prove that economic output grows faster than any computable function of the technological frontier-a property we call supercomputational growth. The result follows from the connection between the technology count H(n) = |T n | and Chaitin's incomputable constant Ω. We establish that the number of available technologies is itself not computable, and that with Dixit-Stiglitz preferences (which exhibit love of variety), output inherits this supercomputational character. We also formalize returns to technological complexity, providing a computational foundation for gains from knowledge combination. The framework exhibits distinct growth regimes-Malthusian trap, industrial takeoff, and sustained growth-with transitions determined by the relationship between technological exploration and population dynamics. The dynamics of exploration and conditions for economic takeoff are deferred to Part IV, where they will be implemented computationally.

title: The Many Shades of Uncertainty and Monetary Policy
affiliations: Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: The Many Shades of Uncertainty and Monetary Policy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 978
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper reviews how different sources of uncertainty influence monetary policy design and transmission. Within a New Keynesian framework, we distinguish between uncertainty arising from non-linearities in the economy and that stemming from imperfect information held by either the central bank or the private sector. While uncertainty is neutral under linearity and full-information rational expectations, departures from these conditions render it consequential for monetary policy. Non-linearities and information frictions alter the optimal degree of policy gradualism and may warrant either more forceful or more cautious responses. The proposed taxonomy offers a structured approach for policy discussions concerning appropriate monetary responses and communication strategies in the face of different types of uncertainty.

title: The use of Robo-Advisors in Italy: Insights from a New Survey
affiliations: Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: The use of Robo-Advisors in Italy: Insights from a New Survey

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 979
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Robo-advisors, the provision of (affordable) financial advice through algorithms on digital platforms, offer great potential to increase participation in financial markets by private individuals. However, like any innovation in finance, opportunities also come with challenges. Based on data from a recent survey of 5,000 individuals, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the characteristics of individuals who use robo-advisors in a country such as Italy, where participation in financial markets is traditionally low, and assess the influence of this technology on the general public’s propensity to make financial investments. Our results show that (i) the adoption of robo-advisors is higher among individuals with greater digital skills but limited financial knowledge; (ii) the adoption of robo-advisors positively influences the propensity to purchase financial assets, such as stocks, bonds, and investment funds.

title: Observational Study of Natural Approaches using Relationship-Driven Theory
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Observational Study of Natural Approaches using Relationship-Driven Theory
detail.abstract: This paper applies the design philosophy of Patent No. 7059476 (Relationship-Driven Theory) to analyze the "inconsistencies" that the natural environment exerts on human civilization. By adopting an engineering perspective, we redefine global systemic inconsistencies-traditionally viewed as mere "natural threats"-as "Controllable Guardrails" within a macro-system. By examining historical human struggles against nature, this study verifies how we can exercise control over these "Upper Nodes." The objective is to describe how the current design philosophy, which treats environmental inconsistencies as errors to be excluded, leads to the stagnation of drive energy, and to propose a new protocol for dynamic coexistence through active refactoring.

title: The Functioning of the Tax Justice System: Microdata Evidence from Italy

detail.title: The Functioning of the Tax Justice System: Microdata Evidence from Italy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 980
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study provides a concise overview of the legal framework governing tax litigation in Italy and documents some stylized facts concerning its functioning, using data on corporate tax disputes. The analyses show that the number of disputes has declined, relative to the early 2010s, partly due to the deflationary effect of the mandatory tax mediation introduced in 2011. On the other hand, the average duration of proceedings and the rate of reversal of decisions between first and second instance have remained broadly stable. By linking litigation data to the financial statements of the population of joint-stock companies, the study identifies factors associated with the incidence of disputes. The analysis reveals a higher concentration of litigation in the manufacturing and trade sectors, as well as in the South. Involvement in tax litigation is associated with a deterioration in corporate performance and with higher exit rates following disputes with negative outcomes, particularly for smaller and more highly indebted firms. The data show a reduction in activity for both successful and unsuccessful firms, suggesting that the uncertainty and costs associated with tax litigation play a significant as well as negative role.

title: Decomposing Migration Drivers: Push-Pull Effects of Political, Financial, and Socioeconomic Institutions Versus Network Effects in OECD Migration

detail.title: Decomposing Migration Drivers: Push-Pull Effects of Political, Financial, and Socioeconomic Institutions Versus Network Effects in OECD Migration

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Journal of Political Economy, volume 93, 2026[10.1016/j.ejpoleco.2026.102810]

detail.abstract: This paper explores the relative importance of key migration drivers and examines how institutional quality influences migration rates using a classical migration model and data from OECD countries over the period 1985-2015. Within a fixed-effects framework, we develop a novel analytical framework using comprehensive institutional quality indices constructed from International Country Risk Guide (ICRG) to capture both pushing and pulling effects. Our variance decomposition analysis reveals that network effects account for 43.73% of the total explained variance in general migration inflows, but only 11.29% for inflow workers and 2.35% for foreign students changing status. Pushing and pulling effects contribute 23.02%and 16.49%, respectively, to general migration inflows, while f or inflow workers, pushing effects dominate, explaining 34.96% compared to 18.78% for pulling effects. Among foreign students changing status, these effects are more balanced, contributing 30.52% and 30.05%, respectively. A deeper analysis of institutional qualities shows that political quality dominate both pushing and pulling effects across most specifications, except for foreign students changing status, where 46.67% of the pulling-effects variance i s explained by socioeconomic factors, compared to 40.68% for political factors. Additionally, geographical distance is the most significant factor in bi lateral migration costs, contributing over 75% across all specifications. These findings help policymakers better understand the complex roles o f networks, institutional qualities, migration costs, etc. in shaping migration patterns.

title: The Resilience of Italy’s External Sector Amidst Risks and Challenges

detail.title: The Resilience of Italy’s External Sector Amidst Risks and Challenges

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 981
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper explores recent macro developments in Italy’s external sector. Despite a succession of adverse shocks and a challenging international context, Italy’s export performance between 2019 and 2024 was quite resilient, overall, boosted by cost competitiveness gains, geographical and sectoral diversification, good quality positioning, the recovery in international tourism, and by growth in business, financial and insurance services. The current account (CA) balance has been persistently positive, with the temporary exception of the 2022 energy crisis. Its more modest level in 2024 (relative to 2019) mainly reflects a weaker investment income balance, due to the higher reactivity of external liabilities to increased interest rates compared with external assets. In our view, the CA balance is broadly in line with fundamentals; external sector resilience is confirmed by a solid creditor net international investment position (NIIP). Looking forward, exports will be negatively impacted by US tariffs, exchange rate appreciation and growing competition from China, although Italy is projected to maintain both a CA surplus and a creditor NIIP in the short term. Over the medium term, the country’s ability to navigate the significant challenges arising from geo-economic fragmentation, the green and digital transitions, and structural changes in world demand will be key to a sound performance.

detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of digital platforms and algorithmic content systems has reshaped the information environment in which children learn, socialize, and form beliefs. Homeschool education, while academically robust in many respects, often lacks structured, research-anchored instruction in algorithmic literacy, digital safety, and cognitive resilience. This gap is especially consequential for learners from historically underserved communities, including Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (DHH) students, who face unique accessibility and information-processing challenges. Drawing on interdisciplinary research in media literacy, digital cognition, and inclusive education, this paper proposes the Public-Aligned AI Homeschool Cognitive Safety Framework-a scalable curriculum model designed to integrate critical algorithmic literacy, media analysis, and cognitive safety within academically equivalent homeschool learning. The framework positions AI literacy not as a replacement for foundational learning but as a harmonized extension required for equitable participation in the digital age.

title: The International Transmission of Chinese Monetary Policy and the Commodity Channel

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1510
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the international transmission of Chinese monetary policy. We show that, unlike the financial channel typical of US monetary policy, Chinese policy shocks propagate through a real-side demand mechanism, driven by monetary-fiscal interactions that stimulate commodity-intensive infrastructure investment. Consistent with this channel, metal and energy commodity prices are the most responsive to Chinese monetary policy shocks. We quantify the resulting inflationary spillovers using counterfactual methods. The commodity channel accounts for approximately 70 per cent of producer price spillovers to advanced economies, with the largest impact concentrated in countries heavily dependent on commodity imports, such as the four largest European economies. Finally, Chinese monetary policy significantly affects financing conditions in commodity-exporting emerging markets.

title: Beyond Belief: Why Institutional Conditions Matter More than Cognition in the Study of Conspiracy Thinking

detail.title: Beyond Belief: Why Institutional Conditions Matter More than Cognition in the Study of Conspiracy Thinking

detail.abstract:
Research on conspiracy thinking has largely centered belief as its primary object of explanation, attributing conspiratorial beliefs to cognitive bias, psychological predisposition, or informational distortion. While this literature has generated important insights into individual-level mechanisms, it has struggled to account for the persistence, diffusion, and cross-context recurrence of conspiratorial beliefs. This article argues that these limitations stem from a mis-specified analytic focus: belief is treated as a causal variable rather than as an outcome shaped by institutional conditions. 
Drawing on a selective review of psychological, sociological, and media-oriented approaches, the article identifies a shared assumption underlying belief-centered modelsthat conspiratorial belief reflects epistemic deficiency rather than responses conditioned by features of the institutional environment. The paper then advances an alternative framing in which conspiracy thinking emerges within contexts characterized by opacity, weak accountability, and narrative insufficiency. Under such conditions, belief correction alone cannot stabilize authoritative interpretation. 
Rather than proposing a comprehensive theory, the article offers a reframing intervention that shifts analytic attention from belief content to the institutional conditions that structure credibility, authority, and interpretive stability. This shift has implications for research design, measurement, and comparative analysis in the study of conspiracy thinking.

detail.abstract: We document that increases in property insurance premiums reduce mortgage originations. The effect is strongest for the rate refinancing and cash-out refinancing segments. We show that denials associated with increased premiums are significantly more likely attributed to high debt-to-income ratios and insufficient collateral. Across the income spectrum, the effect is concentrated among highly levered borrowers. Our results suggest that increases in property insurance premiums could attenuate the refinancing channel of monetary policy as fewer borrowers are able to take advantage of lower rates.

detail.title: Antecedents of risk perception and intention to fly during COVID-19: The role of predetermination, traditionality and trust in authorities
detail.abstract: Despite being significant cultural characteristics, it is believed that there is insufficient information on how predetermination and traditionalism influence trust in authority and risk perception. The COVID-19 pandemic has provided a suitable context for investigating the factors that affect people's perceived risk in the face of hazards and how this risk perception impacts their intention to engage in air travel.,In this study, a comprehensive model was developed to examine how predetermination, traditionalism, and trust in the decisions of authorities within the scope of risk management influence perceived risk, as well as how the intention to engage in air travel is affected by perceived risk and fear arising from this context. The model was tested on 934 Turkish citizens using data obtained from an online survey through the Partial Least Square – Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) method.,The results of the structural equation modeling confirmed the positive impact of predetermination on traditionalism and trust in authority. Additionally, it was revealed that traditionalism mediates the relationship between predetermination and trust in authority, while trust in authority serves as a mediator between predetermination and perceived risk. On the other hand, the findings indicate that perceived risk negatively affects the intention to fly. Furthermore, fear was found to play a negative mediating role between perceived risk and the intention to fly.

title: Inflation Expectations and Price-Setting Decisions: Insights from the Housing Market

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1507
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We investigate how inflation expectations affect pricing decisions in the housing market. We leverage a randomized control trial embedded within an Italian survey of real estate agents and combine survey data for each agent with high-frequency listing prices observed on a large digital platform. Exploiting an exogenous shift in inflation expectations generated by information treatment, we find that higher inflation expectations cause a one-to-one increase in housing listing prices, on average. The pass-through is weaker in more concentrated and low-demand markets, as well as for agents who are more pessimistic about housing and credit developments.

title: EntropyTrack: Attention Entropy Occlusion Detection with Adaptive Multi-Scale Feature Compensation for Robust Visual Tracking
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: EntropyTrack: Attention Entropy Occlusion Detection with Adaptive Multi-Scale Feature Compensation for Robust Visual Tracking
detail.abstract: Robust visual tracking under severe occlusions remains challenging due to the lack of explicit occlusion detection mechanisms and adaptive feature compensation strategies in existing methods. To address this problem, we propose EntropyTrack, a unified transformer-based framework that exploits attention entropy for occlusion-aware tracking. Our approach introduces an Attention Entropy Occlusion Detector that quantifies attention distribution uncertainty to explicitly identify occlusion states with spatial consistency regularization. Building upon this detection, an Adaptive Feature Compensation module performs intelligent feature repair through dynamic fusion of spatial inpainting and temporal information based on detected occlusion patterns. Furthermore, a Multi-Scale Contrastive Learning module enhances feature discriminability via attention-guided sampling across multiple scales for robust target-background separation. Extensive experiments on seven challenging benchmarks including LaSOT, GOT-10k, TrackingNet, LaSOText, VOT2020, TNL2K, and OTB100 demonstrate that EntropyTrack achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining real-time efficiency at 42 fps. The synergistic integration of entropy-driven occlusion detection, adaptive compensation, and multi-scale contrastive learning provides a principled solution for robust visual tracking under challenging conditions.

detail.abstract: We study heterogeneity in household borrowing across nine European countries (Belgium, Spain, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Portugal, and Slovakia) over the 2022-24 period using granular credit register data. We first document substantial between- and within-country variation in mortgage and consumer lending by borrower age, loan maturity, and interest rate fixation. We then quantify the pass-through of the ECB’s recent tightening cycle to household borrowing costs, and assess its heterogeneous impact across households. Pass-through is nearly complete for mortgages (around 0.9) but considerably weaker for consumer credit (around 0.4). While mortgage pass-through is relatively homogeneous across countries, consumer credit shows pronounced cross-country differences that cannot be explained by borrower or loan characteristics. Younger households face stronger mortgage pass-through but weaker consumer credit pass-through, relative to older borrowers, whereas longer maturities are associated with stronger pass-through in both credit markets.

title: Birds of a Feather Flock Together: The Coupling of Innovative Banks and Innovative Firms

detail.abstract: Financial technology (Fintech) innovation in banking has the potential to improve banks’ screening and monitoring abilities, especially for more opaque firms, thereby improving their portfolio and risk allocation. We test the impact of Fintech innovation in borrower monitoring on banks’ supply of credit to Italian firms, with a special focus on small innovative businesses. To this end, we use Credit Register data on outstanding loans for Italy at the bank-firm level, combined with information on bank Fintech innovation from the Bank of Italy’s Regional Bank Lending Survey, and the classification of innovative young firms under the Italian Start-up Act. We find that banks investing in Fintech-based monitoring technologies provide larger volumes of credit to innovative firms at lower interest rates. Moreover, firms borrowing from these banks seem to benefit from stronger relationships, as they are less likely to exit the credit market. Finally, we find no evidence that Fintech innovation in monitoring increases the likelihood of loans to innovative firms becoming non-performing.

title: Can Crises Affect Citizen Activism? Evidence from a Pandemic
affiliations: Indian Statistical Institute, New Delhi - Indian Statistical Institute, affiliation not provided to SSRN, King’s College London and Texas A&M University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Can Crises Affect Citizen Activism? Evidence from a Pandemic
detail.abstract: We ask whether major crises can be catalysts for civic activism. Using state-level variation in COVID-19 peaks in India and quasi-random participation in an online survey (March–July 2021), we measure willingness to act against healthcare fraud by supporting an NGO advocating transparency. Comparing respondents surveyed before and after their state’s COVID-19 peak, we find that exposure to the most acute phase of the pandemic is associated with a greater engagement in low-cost anti-corruption civic actions post-peak. This change coincides with heightened perceptions of healthcare corruption, greater awareness of rights, increased risk tolerance, and more optimistic beliefs about others’ willingness to act. Our findings suggest that exposure to crises can lead to higher levels of low-cost civic actions for accountability.

title: Transaction Costs and the Imperfect Take-up of COVID-19 Business Support Programs
affiliations: Kobe University, Gakushuin University - Economics, Hitotsubashi University, Chuo University and Hitotsubashi University

detail.title: Transaction Costs and the Imperfect Take-up of COVID-19 Business Support Programs
detail.abstract: Not all eligible firms and individuals take up government support measures even when the potential benefits are substantial. This paper investigates why such imperfect take-up arises, focusing on the role of transaction costs in the application process. Employing the data on the use of four COVID-19 business support measures for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Japan combined with firm characteristics, we find that the use of one measure (business continuity grants) causes a discontinuous increase in the use of the other three measures. Our results suggest that the transaction cost involved in applying for these measures plays a vital role, accounting for the relatively low take-up rates of the three measures.

title: Is Old Really Bold? CEO Age and Corporate Risk Management
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University and Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University

detail.title: Is Old Really Bold? CEO Age and Corporate Risk Management
detail.abstract: We examine how CEO age influences corporate risk management by analyzing the usage of foreign exchange (FX) derivatives. Using firm-level data, we find that firms led by older CEOs employ significantly more FX derivatives than those led by younger CEOs, indicating greater risk aversion amongst older CEOs. We also find that older CEOs prefer futures contracts, which are linear derivative instruments that offer greater transparency and lower counterparty risk, indicating a preference for simpler payoff structures and lower risk. This relationship is particularly pronounced in non-high-tech firms, firms with high export exposure, and financially unconstrained firms. Finally, we document that following the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, older CEOs increased their use of FX derivatives, consistent with the idea that heightened regulatory scrutiny heightens risk aversion.

title: Traditional Institutions and Modern Preferences: Evidence from Clan Culture and Old-age Support
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Traditional Institutions and Modern Preferences: Evidence from Clan Culture and Old-age Support
detail.abstract: This paper examines how traditional informal institutions shape preferences for old-age support and the emergence of initiative-based long-term financial planning. Using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study combined with clan genealogy records, we estimate the causal impact of exposure to clan culture on old-age support preferences. We find that stronger exposure to clan culture in early life is associated with a higher likelihood of adopting modern preferences for old-age support, characterized by greater reliance on self-initiated savings and pension participation rather than dependence on children. The results are robust to instrumental variable estimation and placebo test. Importantly, the effect operates exclusively through exposure to clan culture during early life, while clan culture encountered in adulthood has no significant influence, particularly among individuals who relocate later in life. Mechanism analysis suggests that peer effects, generalized trust, income growth, and financial literacy jointly mediate the relationship between clan culture and old-age support preferences. We further show that the expansion of the formal pension system complements, rather than crowds out, the influence of clan culture, consistent with a process of co-evolution between informal and formal institutions. The effects are stronger among individuals with favorable attitudes toward clans, rural residents, and men. Finally, modern preferences induced by clan culture translate into higher pension participation and larger financial asset holdings. Overall, the findings highlight how informal institutions can shape economic preferences and facilitate the adoption of formal financial arrangements.

title: The Impact of AI Exposure on Labor Market Outcomes and Worker Well-Being: Evidence from Australia
affiliations: Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) and Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI)

detail.title: The Impact of AI Exposure on Labor Market Outcomes and Worker Well-Being: Evidence from Australia
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how occupational exposure to artificial intelligence (AI) affects labour market outcomes and worker well-being using longitudinal microdata from the Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey. By following the same individuals for more than two decades (2001–2022), we identify within-person effects of AI exposure while controlling for all time-invariant unobservable characteristics through individual fixed effects. We find mixed labour market and well-being effects. Workers in AI-exposed occupations experience higher hourly wages and greater perceived autonomy in how work is performed, but also report reductions in both usual and desired hours worked, alongside lower satisfaction with job security. Heterogeneity analysis suggests that AI-exposed casual workers faced greater declines in hours and wages, while women saw relative gains in employment and pay, and older workers were less affected in terms of hours. These results remain robust across a range of sensitivity checks, including alternative exposure definitions, placebo tests, pre-2010 exposure restrictions, and comparisons with labour market disruptions related to the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: How AI Shapes Strategic Reasoning: Evidence from Human-Chatbot Dialogue *

detail.title: How AI Shapes Strategic Reasoning: Evidence from Human-Chatbot Dialogue *

declarations.funderStatement: Lu Dong acknowledges financial support from National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant: 72573076 and 72394394) and Social Economics Teaching and Research Center of SUSTECH (SJZLGC202310). detail.abstract: How does access to artificial intelligence affect strategic reasoning in economic decisions? We conduct a pre-registered laboratory experiment with 264 participants making incentivized choices in four canonical games: beauty contest, public goods, ultimatum, and signaling. Participants are randomly assigned to either converse with a large language model through unrestricted conversational support (free-style AI), engage with Feynmanstyle questioning that withholds direct advice (educational AI), or write self-reflections (baseline). We record complete chat transcripts, decisions, and decision explanations. We document three main findings. First, AI access shifts behavior toward payoff maximization, with free-style AI producing larger effects than educational AI. Second, after conversing with AI, game-theoretic and payoff-maximizing arguments increase substantially, while reliance on heuristics and social preferences declines. Third, most chats focus on predicting others' behavior and game-theoretic analysis, with over 90% of AI users seek explicit recommendations. Principal component analysis shows that dialogue features explain a substantial share of decision variance, and semantic analysis further confirms strong correlations between chat content and participants' subsequent decision explanations.

title: Judgment Architecture: Why Innovation and AI Expose Organiztional Decision Limits

detail.title: Judgment Architecture: Why Innovation and AI Expose Organiztional Decision Limits

detail.abstract: AI does not fail primarily because it is inaccurate. It fails because AI systems can only operate on what is spelled out in advance. In everyday organizational work, people constantly make small calls in the moment. They notice when something feels off, check with someone else, or decide to hold back until there is more clarity. These judgments are rarely formalized. They are embedded in shared context, professional norms, escalation habits, and tacit authority structures that have evolved over time. When work is delegated to AI systems, those informal judgment practices do not carry over automatically. AI cannot pause, redirect, or escalate unless those conditions are deliberately designed. As a result, organizations often experience AI failures not because the system behaves unpredictably, but because it behaves exactly as it was allowed to. This paper introduces the concept of judgment as infrastructure to explain this phenomenon. Rather than treating judgment as an individual skill, a governance overlay, or a human-in-the-loop safeguard, the paper argues that judgment functions as a form of organizational infrastructure that must be made visible, explicit, and accountable before work is delegated to machines. The central claim is that many challenges attributed to AI, including loss of control, brittle decision-making, and post-hoc escalation, are symptoms of judgment that was never intentionally designed. AI systems expose these gaps by making delegation irreversible, scalable, and fast, revealing assumptions that previously remained hidden in human coordination. Contribution and Positioning The paper reframes AI-related organizational failure away from model performance and toward the conditions under which delegation occurs. It contributes a conceptual lens that connects AI deployment to organizational design, authority, accountability, and decision rights, while highlighting why existing approaches such as ethical principles, governance committees, and generic human-in-the-loop mechanisms often fail to address the underlying issue. By positioning judgment as infrastructure, the paper opens a new line of inquiry into how organizations design the conditions under which AI systems operate, rather than relying on after-the-fact oversight or individual discretion.

title: Feasibility Study: Blockchain-Based Digital ID in Somalia
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Feasibility Study: Blockchain-Based Digital ID in Somalia
detail.abstract: The National Identification and Registration Authority (NIRA) of Somalia has made significant strides in establishing a foundational national identity system. However, structural limitations, including a highly centralized architecture, fragmented inter-agency interoperability, and persistent data security concerns, threaten its long-term effectiveness, inclusivity, and public trust [1]. This paper, developed from a feasibility study on NIRA's current system, proposes a strategic transition from a basic foundational ID to a Decentralized, Interoperable, and Privacy-Preserving Digital Identity model, leveraging the principles of Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) and blockchain technology. This shift is not primarily a technical upgrade but a governance and coordination challenge [2]. The core recommendation is to implement a secure, permissioned digital identity infrastructure based on W3C standards (Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials). This framework would: 1. Mitigate Centralized Risk: By distributing the verification process and eliminating the single, massive honeypot of personal data. 2. Enhance Interoperability: By enabling all government agencies to securely and instantly verify identity claims using a shared, tamper-proof ledger, transforming NIRA from an operational bottleneck into the authoritative national source of identity trust. 3. Restore Citizen Trust: By granting citizens control over their data, ensuring that personal information is verified selectively rather than copied and stored by multiple agencies. This strategic evolution strengthens NIRA's mandate, supports national inclusion, and establishes a robust digital public infrastructure essential for Somalia's long-term stability and economic growth.

title: Climate Change, State Capacity and Canadian Leadership in Wildfire Mitigation: Strengthening Institutions for a New Era of Climate-Driven Disasters

detail.title: Climate Change, State Capacity and Canadian Leadership in Wildfire Mitigation: Strengthening Institutions for a New Era of Climate-Driven Disasters
detail.abstract: This paper examines the intersection of climate change, state governance capacity, and wildfire mitigation across three income levels. It argues that state capacity—measured through institutional frameworks, technological resources, and fiscal investment—fundamentally shapes nations' ability to respond to climate-driven disasters, particularly wildfires. Through comparative analysis of Canada (high-income), Brazil (middle-income), and Indonesia (lower-middle-income), the study demonstrates that while wealth enables resources, institutional coordination, legal frameworks, and community engagement are equally critical. Canada's record 2023 and 2025 wildfire seasons (17.5M and 8.8M hectares burned) exposed both advanced state capacity (international cooperation, modernized funding) and vulnerabilities. The paper proposes five domestic strategies—modernized legislation, technology investment, community resilience, Indigenous co-management, and a national wildfire agency—and three international recommendations—Pan-American cooperation, standardized protocols, and a Global Center for Research. By integrating scientific expertise with Indigenous knowledge and establishing transnational frameworks, Canada can position itself as a leader in climate adaptation, providing a replicable blueprint for nations facing unprecedented wildfire threats. This research contributes to policy analysis and disaster governance literature by demonstrating how institutional innovation, combined with international collaboration, strengthens climate resilience.

title: Epistemic Justice in Construction Research: Re-evaluating Performance Metrics for Construction Management and Quantity Surveying

detail.title: Epistemic Justice in Construction Research: Re-evaluating Performance Metrics for Construction Management and Quantity Surveying
detail.abstract: Construction Management (CM) and Quantity Surveying (QS) are practice-intensive disciplines that address complex, value-laden challenges in the built environment. Despite their societal relevance-from climate-resilient infrastructure to ethical labor practices-they remain epistemologically marginalized in research assessment systems dominated by positivist, laboratory-based norms. This paper argues that the current application of universal key performance indicators (KPIs)-such as journal impact factors, citation counts, and grant income-to CM and QS constitutes a form of epistemic injustice. Drawing on critical realism, Mode 2 knowledge production, and an axiologically grounded philosophy of research, we demonstrate that CM and QS generate knowledge through situated, transdisciplinary, and ethically reflective processes that cannot be fairly captured by metrics designed for natural sciences or theoretical engineering. We propose a reconfigured evaluation framework anchored in the author's "Research Philosophical Onion," which positions ontology (what exists as real in construction) and axiology (the role of values) as foundational outer layers guiding all methodological choices. The paper concludes with actionable recommendations for universities, accreditation bodies (e.g., CIOB, RICS), and national research councils to implement discipline-sensitive assessment criteria that honor the unique urgency, output forms, and intellectual contributions of CM and QS scholarship.

detail.abstract: The rapid digitalization of India's travel industry has made algorithmic decisions systems the main tool for price determination which creates new competition law problems. This article critically examines two separates yet connected risks which results from technological advancement they are Device Based Price Discrimination (DPD) where platforms leverage granular user data such as Android vs iOS, and Algorithmic Collusion (AC) where selflearning price tools coordinate to fix prices without explicit human communication. Evaluates the Competition Act,2002 to reveal major weaknesses in its current enforcement system. This article examines Section 3 evidence requirement for algorithmic tacit collusion through the Competition Commission of India's denial of a "Hub & Spoke" conspiracy in Samir Agrwal v. Competition Commission of India. Conversely, the article also analyzes the MakeMyTrip-Goibibo ruling to show how Section 4 helps to address abuse of dominance through vertical market restrictions and parity clause. Ultimately, article demonstrates that traditional ex-post enforcement regime fails to manage the velocity and opacity of the "black box" algorithm. This article advocates for a paradigm shift towards ex-ante regulation and enhanced evidence collection methods to safeguard consumer welfare and ensure competition in India's digital economy.

title: A Strategy-First, Rule-Based Decision Support System for Equity Market Analysis

detail.title: A Strategy-First, Rule-Based Decision Support System for Equity Market Analysis
detail.abstract: This work proposes an Equity Strategy Assistant designed as a decision-support system for equity strategy formulation, simulation, and market condition monitoring. The system is explicitly constructed to assist human users in reasoning about trading ideas through structured representation, rule-based evaluation, and explanatory analysis, without participating in or influencing execution decisions. At its core, the system supports the transformation of informal trading concepts into explicit, inspectable strategy definitions, enabling users to test those definitions against historical data and observe how they interact with real or delayed market conditions. The system does not act autonomously, nor does it optimize for financial outcomes. Instead, it functions as an analytical aid that helps users understand what happened, under which conditions, and why-while leaving all interpretive and execution authority with the human user. The design deliberately prioritizes transparency, auditability, and constraint over predictive power. Automated components are used to evaluate rule satisfaction, simulate outcomes, and summarize behavior, but they are intentionally restricted from producing recommendations or prescriptive actions. Human judgment remains central throughout the decision-making process.

detail.abstract: In May 2023, two floods hit the Italian region of Emilia-Romagna, causing 17 deaths and €10 billion in damages. This paper investigates the impact of such floods on economic activity and household wealth. Using nightlight data to measure economic activity and considering a triple difference-in-differences empirical framework, we find a decline in nightlight activity in flooded municipalities in the three weeks surrounding the two floods, a rebound effect in the following three weeks, but no effect thereafter. In the most pessimistic scenario, the total reduction in regional GDP growth in 2023 is between 0.1 and 0.2 per cent, i.e. between €3 and 5 million, excluding the agricultural sector. The duration of the impact of the floods is broadly confirmed by the other two proxies for economic activity available at the daily frequence and municipal level, i.e. hiring and road traffic data. We also find temporary effects on the housing market demand, but no effects on the house prices asked by the sellers nor on the number of posted advertisements for house sales, suggesting that the housing market in flooded municipalities already discounts the risk of such natural events.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the structural mechanisms of wealth extraction in the United States economy from 1971 to 2026, challenging the dominant narrative that attributes middle-class economic stagnation to foreign competition. Through analysis of wage stagnation patterns, asset concentration data, interlocking ownership structures, and shadow banking architecture, we demonstrate that domestic institutional capture-not external economic forces-represents the primary driver of wealth redistribution from labor to capital. We conclude that the enemy of American prosperity has never been foreign, but rather a domestic architecture of extraction that operates through legal, monetary, and institutional channels.

detail.abstract: Thousands of diseases lack FDA-approved treatments, and at current research capacity, it will take centuries to explore potential therapies. We propose redirecting just 1% of global military spending ($27.2 billion annually) to pragmatic clinical trials. This investment would increase trial capacity more than 12-fold, accelerating treatment discovery by over two centuries. The timeline shift would prevent 10.7 billion deaths over the long term, valued at $84.8 quadrillion. detail.abstract: This paper examines the effects of shrinking fiscal space and the resulting fiscal consolidation on private and public expenditure in research and development (R&D). In a sample of OECD countries, we find R&D expenditure strongly influenced by the available fiscal space, with this relationship being particularly pronounced in less innovative countries. To better understand this relationship, we further explore a potential transmission channel: fiscal consolidation. Our analysis shows that the spending cuts in public allocations to R&D driven by fiscal adjustments are more pronounced in less innovative countries, suggesting the presence of a doom loop between consolidations and low domestic R&D intensity. detail.abstract: This paper investigates the causal effects of a competitive excellence initiative financing Italy’s top twenty-five per cent university departments. detail.abstract:
Executive Summary

The federal Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) program delivered $200 billion nationally between 2020-2025, including $7.8 billion for Illinois, to stabilize school operations during COVID-19, address learning loss, expand digital access, support student mental health, reduce class sizes, and sustain critical staffing. The expiration of this funding marks a pivotal turning point in K–12 education finance. Districts serving low-income students relied heavily on ESSER to launch and scale tutoring programs, extended learning opportunities, counseling services, and literacy initiatives that helped narrow post-pandemic achievement gaps. These districts now face mounting fiscal pressures that threaten to reverse hard-won gains. This Policy Brief examines ESSER’s sunset impact on the 2025–2026 school year and identifies state policy options to sustain its most effective interventions.

What did Illinois districts spend ESSER funding on, and what progress was made?

ESSER funds in Illinois have primarily been directed toward five focal areas (Illinois State Board of Education, 2025):

  •     Expanding tutoring and intervention programs to address learning loss
  •     Investing in technology and broadband access for remote learning
  •     Enhancing mental health and social-emotional support services
  •     Hiring additional staff and reducing class sizes
  •     Implementing COVID-19 safety protocols in school buildings       

While comprehensive impact evaluation continues, available data show positive relationships between ESSER investment and student outcomes. Illinois districts allocating approximately 45% of ESSER funds to staffing maintained higher math and reading achievement on IAR and SAT assessments during the pandemic, while districts investing only 3% in staffing experienced larger achievement declines and slower recovery (Cashdollar et al., 2024).

Chicago Public Schools exemplifies these patterns. Serving 17% of Illinois students (90% students of color, 71% low-income), CPS experienced larger pandemic-related achievement declines than the state average but demonstrated faster recovery rates in both IAR reading and math (Barragan Torres et al., 2024).

What are the implications?

With ESSER funding expired and Illinois facing budget challenges, districts that expanded tutoring, hired counselors and social workers, and reduced class sizes with federal dollars are now scaling back (ISBE, 2024). In turn, many districts expect larger class sizes, with many anticipating hiring delays or position losses (Smylie, 2025). Education stakeholders are watching how these changes affect student outcomes, especially for populations that benefited most from expanded services (FutureEd, 2024).

The analysis relies on information from the Regional Bank Lending Survey on the supply of digital services by Italian banks and on data from the Survey on Household Income and Wealth regarding households’ use of remote connections with banks. The use of digital channels is more widespread among households with greater economic resources and where the main income earner has a higher level of education and stronger financial and digital skills; conversely, it is negatively associated with the main income earner’s age. The use of digital banking also increases among households whose relationship with the financial system is more complex (in terms of, e.g. having connections with multiple banks, investing in financial assets, or holding debt). title: Mechanization as Insurance: Evidence from Nepal's Plains

detail.title: Mechanization as Insurance: Evidence from Nepal's Plains
detail.abstract: Mechanization service markets have expanded rapidly across South Asia, allowing even very small farms to rent machinery. Using household data from Nepal, we examine whether mechanization improves farm profitability or primarily mitigates risk. We estimate scale-interacted efficiency and risk models using net farm income outcomes. Mechanization intensity shows no significant association with net farm income per hectare for the smallest landholders but generates strong positive returns for mid-sized farms In contrast, higher mechanization intensity significantly reduces the probability of negative net farm income across all farm sizes. These findings indicate that mechanization functions primarily as an insurance mechanism for smallholders facing labor scarcity rather than as a pathway to income growth. The results highlight the importance of scale in determining returns to service-based mechanization and suggest that access alone is insufficient to generate productivity gains among the smallest farms.

detail.abstract: In-kind transfers, such as healthcare and education services, represent a substantial portion of public expenditure in most advanced economies, yet they are rarely included in analyses of tax-benefit systems due to the methodological challenges in assessing their monetary value. This paper adds an in-kind transfer module to an otherwise standard microsimulation model of the Italian household sector. Following established methodologies, we evaluate the health, education, childcare, and social housing services enjoyed by each beneficiary. We find that in-kind benefits follow a distinctively U-shaped age profile and are more uniformly distributed across income levels compared to cash benefits. In-kind transfers increase net disposable income by 20 percent, on average, and almost 60 per cent for lower-income households, therefore playing a crucial role in reducing inequality. These results confirm the importance of including in-kind transfers in distributional analyses for a more complete understanding of welfare systems.

detail.abstract:
This Article presents a governance framework for limited liability companies that addresses a pervasive structural issue in American LLC law: the disconnect between ex ante transactional drafting and ex post regulatory, audit, and judicial scrutiny. While operating agreements are generally afforded broad deference under modern LLC statutes, courts and regulators frequently reconstruct control, fiduciary compliance, and economic substance retrospectively. This practice exposes the inadequacy of purely contractual solutions in contexts where non-waivable statutory duties impose mandatory governance requirements.

The Article introduces a five-layer audit-safe governance framework—comprising Narrative, Schedule, Exhibit, Appendix, and Interpretive layers—intended to align private ordering with the evidentiary standards applied by courts and federal auditors. The framework is specifically designed to accommodate trust-integrated ownership structures, addressing audit vulnerabilities that emerge when beneficial interests are separated from operational control. Each layer serves a distinct function in countering control-by-conduct arguments, documenting independent economic activity, and establishing contemporaneous business purpose.

By situating the framework within South Carolina's Limited Liability Company Act and recent appellate decisions, the Article demonstrates that cases such as Park Regency, Historic Charleston Holdings v. Mallon, and Boathouse at Breach Inlet exemplify a judicial willingness to reconstruct LLC control based on substantive realities rather than formal documentation. South Carolina's mandatory fiduciary provisions render purely contractual approaches doctrinally vulnerable.

The framework's evidentiary architecture is broadly applicable and not limited to a single jurisdiction. Mandatory duties of good faith and fair dealing persist across Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act jurisdictions, and even contractarian regimes such as Delaware increasingly examine whether governance structures reflect economic reality. By treating South Carolina as the highest common denominator, where judicial reconstruction is most rigorous, the Article positions the framework as a national model for audit-resilient LLC governance.

title: The Blown Head Gasket Effect: Rise and struggles of The Drivers Cooperative in New York City

detail.title: The Blown Head Gasket Effect: Rise and struggles of The Drivers Cooperative in New York City
detail.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth case study of The Drivers Cooperative (TDC), a driver-owned ride-hailing platform based in New York City, to examine the challenges faced by multistakeholder platform cooperatives. Drawing on 16 semi-structured interviews, six months of participant observation, and extensive desk research, the study traces how TDC’s growth efforts ultimately led to a fracture between its cooperative membership and its platform infrastructure. This dynamic – conceptualised as the Blown Head Gasket Effect – illustrates how diverging stakeholders can fracture during the development of democratic platform alternatives. Factors such as limited access to capital, political divergence among stakeholders, and temporal pressures are identified as key drivers of this effect. The paper concludes by discussing TDC’s legislative achievements and offering practical recommendations for cooperative practitioners and policy interventions. By situating TDC within broader debates on platform cooperativism and the digital solidarity economy, the study underscores the importance of learning from defeats to enhance cooperative business resilience.

detail.abstract: Empirical studies in econophysics, notably by Yakovenko (2000), have identified a robust "tworegime" structure in income and wealth distributions: an exponential Boltzmann-Gibbs bulk encompassing the majority of the population, followed by a Pareto power-law tail. While stochastic models successfully reproduce these statistical patterns through additive and multiplicative dynamics, they offer limited insight into the structural mechanism underlying the transition between the two regimes. This paper proposes a geometric and thermodynamic interpretation within the EMIS (Energy-Matter-Information-Spacetime) framework. Adopting an analytical analogy rather than asserting a literal physical equivalence, we model money as a conserved flow variable and capital as a form of accumulated structural constraint. Within this representation, the lower-income regime corresponds to a thermal phase governed by maximum-entropy dynamics, whereas the upper tail emerges as an accretion-dominated regime driven by structural amplification. We show that the transition from the exponential to the power-law distribution can be interpreted as a geometric phase transition, in which sufficient structural accumulation alters the effective economic metric and enables self-reinforcing growth. Under this view, persistent poverty arises as a maximum-entropy equilibrium of unstructured exchange, while wealth concentration appears as a symmetry-breaking outcome associated with structural curvature. By reframing wealth distribution through a unified geometric lens, this work provides a generative mechanism linking statistical regularities, inequality persistence, and capital accumulation, and serves as a methodological foundation for subsequent domain-specific analyses within the EMIS framework.
