detail.abstract: Concern persists that pathogens attaching to microplastics (MPs) may spread farther in rivers and elevate public health risks. Yet whether pathogen flux carried on riverine MP substantially augments transport via river water is unknown. We quantified, under global river conditions, the fraction of pathogen transport attributable to MP attachment. Riverine MP concentrations were simulated with the MARINA-Plastics model and pathogen concentrations with the GloWPa model at a global sub-basin resolution. We assessed Cryptosporidium worldwide and Escherichia coli (E. coli) for China at the same sub-basin resolution. For the first time, outputs from MP and pathogen models were integrated to estimate MP-pathogen binding probabilistically across rivers. Attachment was represented with an empirical Freundlich sorption formulation parameterized from literature data. Predicted MP-bound E. coli concentrations exceeded those of Cryptosporidium, reflecting stronger sorption and higher bacterial abundances. Despite this, MP-associated pathogens constituted only a negligible share of riverine pathogen transport fluxes, implying that MP contributes little to pathogen-related public health impacts at the scales considered. The framework can be extended to evaluate risks from hazardous particles and co-transported contaminants, including other pathogens, metals, and organic chemicals, to inform evidence-based policy and monitoring priorities.

title: Mathematical Foundations of Organizational Thermodynamics: Non-smooth Dynamics, Differential Inclusions, and the Bifurcation of Survival
affiliations: Otaru University of Commerce - Department of Economics

detail.title: Mathematical Foundations of Organizational Thermodynamics: Non-smooth Dynamics, Differential Inclusions, and the Bifurcation of Survival
detail.abstract: This paper establishes the rigorous mathematical foundations for the "Grand Unified Equation" of Organizational Thermodynamics proposed in the author's preceding pentalogy. While previous models described the organization as a dissipative structure governed by the Schrödinger Condition, the governing equation contains a discontinuous signum function, sgn(ΔL), representing the discrete nature of structural transformation costs. Consequently, standard theories of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) fail to guarantee the existence of solutions at the switching surface ΔL = 0. By reformatting the system as a Differential Inclusion and applying the concept of convex sets to the discontinuity, we prove the existence of solutions even at singular points. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the lack of uniqueness at the origin provides the mathematical basis for "Strategic Bifurcation," proving that organizational survival is not deterministic but a stochastic choice between "Stagnation (Heat Death)" and "Innovation (Negentropy Intake)".

detail.abstract: The Equation of Exchange, M V = P Y , proposed by Irving Fisher, is foundational to monetary economics. However, it is typically treated as an accounting identity rather than a derived law. A dimensional puzzle exists: if monetary flow is analogous to energy transport, why is the equation linear in velocity (V) rather than quadratic (V 2), as in kinetic energy? We resolve this puzzle by positing that economic activity occurs on a 2-dimensional topological manifold (a transaction network) rather than in 3D Euclidean space. On such a manifold, the governing conservation law is the Continuity Equation for mass flux, which is linear in velocity. We derive the Fisher Equation as the integrated form of this conservation law, providing a first-principles physical foundation for a central result in macroeconomics.

title: Bailouts and Financial Fragility Revisited
affiliations: University of Vienna

detail.title: Bailouts and Financial Fragility Revisited
detail.abstract: When should governments limit their ability to bail out financial institutions? Conventional wisdom holds that bailouts (and public backstops in general) improve welfare when they are the least-bad option during crises and when moral hazard is minimal or contained by ex ante regulation. We revisit this question in a Diamond-Dybvig model with limited commitment, fiscal policy, and endogenous run risk. We show that even when bailouts are ex post efficient and moral hazard is fully eliminated, allowing them can raise the likelihood of bank runs and reduce ex ante welfare, especially when fiscal space is tight.

detail.title: Bank CEO Compensation, Systemic Risk, and Bonus Caps
detail.abstract: Using a new dataset on U.S. bank CEO compensation, I document that pre-crisis cash bonus incentives are associated with worse performance and greater bankruptcy risk during the Global Financial Crisis, whereas option incentives are weaker. To interpret these patterns and evaluate policy, I estimate a dynamic banking model with a multi-component CEO contract in which bonuses are small relative to equity but tied to short-term revenue. In the model, revenue-linked bonuses increase correlated risk-taking, and capping bonuses at base salary with deferral reduces crisis-period failures by about 10%, at the cost of 1% lower lending and 2% lower bank value.

title: Heat Stress and Gendered Time Allocation: Evidence from India

detail.abstract: This paper examines how short-term heat stress, measured by deviations in wetbulb temperature (WBT), affects daily time allocation in India, with a focus on gender, caregiving responsibilities, and the spatial context of work. We combine the nationally representative India Time Use Survey (TUS) - 2019 with high-resolution ERA5 climate reanalysis data to construct district-day WBT anomalies relative to a 2008–2018 baseline. Our empirical strategy exploits within-district, within-month variation in WBT and clusters standard errors at the district level to isolate behavioral responses to acute thermal stress. We find consistent gender asymmetries in responses to rising heat. In the baseline specification, a one-unit (1◦C) increase in WBT leads women to spend 3.03 additional minutes per day on unpaid work and 5.87 fewer minutes on paid work relative to men. Among the already employed subgroup, the reallocation is sharper: women shift 4.08 minutes into unpaid work and 5.72 minutes out of paid work per 1◦C. Parenthood further amplifies these disparities in unpaid labor: at zero children, the same increase in wet bulb raises women’s unpaid work by 6.55 minutes more than men’s, with the additional burden growing by 4.63 minutes for each child. In contrast, the paid work penalty diminishes with parenthood: women without children reduce paid work by 8.95 minutes more than men, but this gap narrows by 3.22 minutes per child. We document heterogeneity by the location of activity and conducted Placebo tests to supporting the validity of our identification strategy. Rising WBT increases women’s time within household premises and reduces time in non-fixed outdoor work, consistent with heat-avoidance behavior. We also examine heterogeneity by social group and find no statistically significant differences in temperature responsiveness across caste categories. The findings indicate that heat stress reduces women’s market participation while raising their domestic labor burden, reinforcing pre-existing gender inequalities in time allocation. These results underscore the need for gender-responsive climate adaptation policies that address the hidden time costs of environmental stress, including investments in care infrastructure and labor protections for vulnerable groups.

detail.abstract: LLMs achieve strong results on local code completion and small bug fixes, yet production engineering work frequently requires repository scale reasoning where the root cause is far from the symptom. We frame these settings as a needle in a haystack problem: the haystack is a large repository, and the needle is the minimal critical information, often an invariant, configuration gate, or cross module dependency required for a correct fix. We conduct an empirical study of long horizon coding tasks on real codebases, evaluating tool using LLM agents that search, inspect files, propose patches, and run tests under fixed interaction budgets. Across models, failures are dominated by missed needles and hypothesis lock in, while implementation errors are less common once the relevant evidence is found. These results motivate process aware evaluation metrics and agent designs that prioritize structured exploration, belief revision, and verification driven iteration.

title: Closed-Loop Valuation Systems: From Permissive Estimation to Structural Economic Proof

detail.title: Closed-Loop Valuation Systems: From Permissive Estimation to Structural Economic Proof
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a closed-loop valuation system that reframes valuation from a permissive estimation exercise into a structurally governed economic process. Unlike traditional valuation frameworks-where assumptions may compensate for one another and valuation outcomes are almost always produced-the proposed system enforces capital preservation, performance precedence, cash-flow sufficiency, temporal discipline, and multi-path convergence as mandatory conditions for value recognition. By embedding structural refusal as a valid outcome, the framework restores economic legitimacy to valuation practice and aligns valuation with institutional, fiduciary, and credit-sensitive decision-making. This manuscript is presented as a conceptual and structural research work. It does not aim to produce firm-specific valuation outputs, but to redefine valuation as a governed economic system.

detail.abstract:
This working paper delivers a comprehensive examination of the European Union's (EU’s) strategic partnerships with Brazil, the United Kingdom, the United States, Russia,Turkey and China.

For each case study, it explores the historical origins and current state of these partnerships, the different forms they can take, and the objectives and challenges they seek to address.

By zooming in on critical policy areas of each relationship and the role of EU Member States therein, the paper sheds light on the horizontal and vertical coherence of the EU’s external action.

The case studies show the importance of recognising each strategic partnership's unique regional and global context, which is indissociable from the EU’s bilateral relationship with the third country.

The successes, failures or stagnations of these relationships cannot be attributed solely to the EU’s policies or lack thereof, as external factors and the partners' own actions and policies can significantly influence the outcomes.

It is argued that strategic partnerships have the potential to establish lasting frameworks for joint action, create momentum for further cooperation, and sustain important relationships amidst potential crises and unforeseen events.

However, the partnerships must demonstrate adaptability to geopolitical and geoeconomic changes while maintaining their alignment with the EU’s external action objectives.

title: India's Health Financing Crisis and the Ayushman Bharat Scheme as a PPP Response

detail.abstract: India's rapid economic growth is challenged by a health financing crisis that has been marked by a typically high out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE), causing limited financial protection, inequality and access to health services among the poorer populations. While the flagship Ayushman Bharat scheme intends to bridge the gap, there still exist a lot of institutional barriers that have blocked the scheme from fulfilling its objectives and outcomes. The OOPE remains high, while the missing middle is a problem within the section of society who are not poor enough to qualify for subsidized healthcare and are unable to access quality healthcare. This paper aims to assess the effectiveness of the Ayushman Bharat scheme through a comparative policy analysis. The paper compares the Ayushman Bharat schemes with the policy structures in 4 other countries, namely Indonesia, the United Kingdom, Brazil, and Mexico. The paper finds its theoretical foundation in evolutionary theory while its methodological framework depends on the idea of critical multiplism. The paper deploys the use of quantitative comparative analysis as well as index-based comparison along with Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021) difference-indifferences with multiple time periods to understand the efficacy of a PPP model on the longer run.

title:
Follow the Cheese:
Pastoralism and Rural Change in Contemporary Turkey

detail.title:
Follow the Cheese:
Pastoralism and Rural Change in Contemporary Turkey

publicationDetails.detailsText: This doctoral thesis was written in the Political Science Doctoral Program at Hacettepe University between 2020 and 2024. The data used is based on fieldwork and archival research.

detail.abstract: This study aims to examine the relationship between pastoralism and rural change in contemporary Turkey with a particular attention to the production and marketing of two famous kinds of cheese, namely tulum and kaşar identified mostly with the pastoralist tribes. There are many challenges to studying pastoralism, an area that has been largely overlooked by both policy makers and social scientists. In order to overcome these, I used both archival research and fieldwork. I limited my multi-sited fieldwork to Erzincan and Kars, and with the new connections I made, I extended it to Tunceli and Ardahan. In these areas, I interviewed members of the Şavaks and Karapapaks. The common characteristic of these pastoralist tribes is that they are also the main producers of two well-known cheese in Turkey. Since my research is shaped by the discussion of how to understand rural change through pastoralism, I first go into how pastoralism has been analyzed conceptually and historically in the existing literature. Then, I shed light on the social, economic, and ecological characteristics of the region and cities I study. Through an innovative conceptual approach to the data obtained from the interviews I analyze it as complaint transcript and assessed how pastoralists position themselves as subjects and how they conceive the state. Subsequently, the constitution of highlands is examined in their conceptual and legal development; highlands are a prerequisite for the existence of pastoralists. Applying findings from both fieldwork and local periodicals, I address the discrepancy between legal and normative perspectives, specifically the question of what constitutes the reality on the ground. Another original contribution of this thesis is the conceptualization of the cities of Kars and Erzincan as cheese lands, with special attention to the role of these tribes in the urban contexts, using the concept of terroir.

title: Efficiency Dynamics of Indian Public Sector Banks postliberalisation: A DEA and Tobit Analysis (1991-2024)

detail.title: Efficiency Dynamics of Indian Public Sector Banks postliberalisation: A DEA and Tobit Analysis (1991-2024)
detail.abstract: This study examines the operational efficiency and reform-induced performance dynamics of Indian public sector banks in the post-liberalisation era. We use Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) under Constant and Variable Returns to Scale to evaluate the trends in technical, pure technical, and scale efficiency over the period 1991-2024, with particular emphasis on the impact of large-scale bank mergers. A second-stage Tobit regression model is employed to identify the financial determinants influencing efficiency scores during 1996-2024. The results reveal persistent input-oriented inefficiencies in the pre-merger period, followed by a marked improvement in efficiency and convergence among banks after consolidation. Capital adequacy emerges as the most significant positive determinant of efficiency, highlighting the role of strong capitalisation in enhancing operational performance. In contrast, return on assets exhibits a statistically significant and negative association with efficiency, while bank size shows a negative but statistically insignificant relationship. The findings provide empirical evidence on the effectiveness of banking reforms and consolidation policies in improving the efficiency of public sector banks in India, and offer policy-relevant insights for strengthening resilience, resource allocation, and long-term stability in the public banking system.

title: Three Drivers of High-Risk Speculation Among Younger Adults: Moral Stigma, Insufficient Financial Curriculum, and Social Media Influence

detail.title: Three Drivers of High-Risk Speculation Among Younger Adults: Moral Stigma, Insufficient Financial Curriculum, and Social Media Influence
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a conceptual framework for why younger adults (20–39) increasingly enter financial markets through relatively high-risk, speculative channels in the post-2015 period. It begins with a sustained gap between asset-price growth and wage growth, which can make capital income more salient for life-cycle accumulation. The core issue is not participation itself but whether entrants have sufficiently developed financial literacy and decision-making frameworks. The framework integrates three forces: (i) moral stigma toward capital income that can undermine the perceived legitimacy of learning about investing and returns, (ii) weak or misaligned financial curricula that constrain financial literacy formation, and (iii) social media dynamics that amplify risk-taking incentives through attention-driven content, investment spectrum narrowing, and flex culture. The argument is interpretive rather than causal and draws on visual time-series evidence. It outlines plausible mechanisms and offers brief cross-country illustrations centered on the United States and South Korea. It concludes with testable propositions and discusses policy implications for public communication, curriculum reform, and investor education in attention-ranked platforms.

detail.abstract: We study how central bank communication about the uncertainty surrounding its assessment of macroeconomic developments shapes financial market reactions to economic news. Using euro-area evidence, we show that when markets perceive the central bank to be operating in a “high-learning” regime – marked by high uncertainty and repeated forecast errors – the pass-through of inflation surprises to interest rates is amplified, resulting in greater volatility. To interpret these findings, we develop a model of imperfect information in which the private sector updates its beliefs about the persistent component of inflation using both realized inflation and the central bank’s projections. In this setting, the central bank’s projections are viewed act as noisy signals, and their perceived precision determines how much weight the private sector places on the central bank’s macroeconomic assessment relative to incoming data. The model predicts that when projections are viewed as more precise, expectations become more anchored and interest rates respond less to news. Overall, the empirical and theoretical results highlight that communicating the confidence surrounding central bank projections is not a neutral act of transparency but an active policy instrument.

detail.title: Bounding Age-Period-Cohort Effects in Travel Behavior: Addressing the Identification Problem Using Theoretically and Empirically Grounded Constraints
detail.abstract: Age-period-cohort (APC) analyses are increasingly used in transportation research to study travel behavior and how it changes over time. Yet conventional APC approaches rely on strong identifying assumptions that are often not made explicit by the researchers and may be difficult to justify. This paper introduces the APC bounding approach proposed by Fosse and Winship (2019b) to transportation research and assesses its suitability through an empirical application to car-use outcomes. Using repeated cross-sectional data from the German travel survey Mobilität in Deutschland (MiD), including the post-pandemic wave 2023, we derived theory- and/or evidence-based bounding assumptions on the age, period, and cohort slopes and combined them with identified nonlinearities to obtain bounded overall effects. We further adapted the approach to a Two-part model to distinguish between participation in car use on the reference day, car-use intensity (kilometers travelled), and total expected kilometers (including zeros). Results for total expected car kilometers (including zeros) show that the post-pandemic decrease is driven by declining participation, despite ambiguous period effects on car use intensity. The bounded cohort effects remain relatively wide for the most recent cohorts but indicate increasing car use intensity while participation remains stable or slightly decreases. Overall, APC bounding improves transparency by making the identifying assumptions explicit and by supporting sensitivity analyses. However, its suitability for transportation research is limited by the method’s requirements to construct equally spaced age-period-cohort bins, the presence of theoretically and/or empirically grounded constraints, and by the fact that the current implementation is tied to linear regression models.

detail.abstract: The global artificial intelligence ecosystem stands at the precipice of a fundamental structural realignment, a transition so profound that it differentiates the era of experimentation (2022-2025) from the era of industrialization (2026-2030). Our comprehensive analysis of venture capital flows, technical adoption curves, and enterprise implementation data confirms the hypothesis: Q4 2026 will mark the definitive inflection point where the "thin wrapper" economy collapses under the weight of diminishing returns, while the "sovereign application layer" and "AI service" sectors ascend to dominance. title: From Digital Policy to Execution Sovereignty Europe's Strategic Foresight in an Era of Machine-Speed Governance Author

detail.abstract: European digital regulation has developed into one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks in the world, covering data protection, artificial intelligence, platform governance, financial integrity, and cybersecurity. However, enforcement mechanisms remain predominantly ex-post, policy-based, and institutionally slow, while the systems they govern increasingly operate at machine speed and across borders. This paper argues that Europe's next strategic inflection point is not further regulatory expansion, but execution sovereignty: the capacity to ensure that legally constrained digital actions cannot execute unless legality, purpose, and jurisdiction are satisfied at the moment of execution. The paper proposes a strategic foresight shift from data localisation and retrospective accountability toward execution-time enforcement, enabling democratic resilience, SME competitiveness, and digital sovereignty without censorship, surveillance, or fragmentation of the global digital ecosystem. The analysis draws on European policy processes, implementation failures, and emerging risks in AI-driven, automated systems. It outlines a coherent foresight framework for the period 2026-2035 and positions execution-time enforcement as Europe's distinctive contribution to global digital governance.

detail.abstract: The protracted armed conflict in Cameroon's English-speaking NorthWest and SouthWest regions has, since 2016, generated a large population of internally displaced persons (IDPs), most of whom are women and children. Forced to flee their homes and livelihoods, these IDPs face severe humanitarian, social, and economic challenges within host communities already marked by poverty and limited access to basic services. This article critically examines the protection afforded to internally displaced persons in the context of the Anglophone crisis, with a particular focus on measures adopted by the Cameroonian State and its partners. Anchored in the triple-pronged theory of state obligations to respect, protect, and fulfil human rights, the study argues that IDPs are entitled to enjoy their rights on an equal basis with other citizens, especially in situations of vulnerability arising from armed conflict. Using a doctrinal and descriptive approach, the article analyses key state initiatives, including the reconstruction process, the Major National Dialogue, peace and reconciliation efforts, the establishment of institutions such as the National Commission for the Promotion of Bilingualism and Multiculturalism and the Disarmament, Demobilization and Reintegration Committee, as well as social, economic, and health-related interventions aimed at alleviating the plight of IDPs. It further assesses collaborative efforts with humanitarian actors and non-governmental organizations under frameworks such as the Humanitarian Response Plan. The article finds that while notable measures have been adopted, implementation gaps, limited coverage, and sustainability challenges continue to undermine effective protection. It concludes by underscoring the need for more coherent, adequately resourced, and rights-based responses to ensure durable solutions for internally displaced persons in Cameroon's conflict-affected regions.

title: Political Persistence of Redistribution: Dependence, Inequality, and Long-Run Income Dynamics

detail.title: Political Persistence of Redistribution: Dependence, Inequality, and Long-Run Income Dynamics
detail.abstract: This paper studies the long-run effects of redistribution using an agent-based model with heterogeneous productivity and education. Agents receive proportional income taxation and uniform transfers, while productivity evolves endogenously as a function of accumulated government dependence and tax burden. We show that strengthening redistribution can generate a gradual but persistent decline in aggregate income, even as income inequality falls. The key mechanism is the endogenous accumulation of dependence, which nonlinearly erodes labor incentives over time and operates beyond standard static labor-supply elasticities. In the simulations, higher redistribution makes all education groups-including the median household-poorer in absolute terms, and alters the productive composition of the economy toward lower-productivity agents. These results are robust across alternative parameterizations, population sizes, and time horizons. The findings caution against evaluating redistributive policies solely on short-run distributional outcomes and highlight the importance of dynamic incentive effects for long-run prosperity.

title: Aging, Political Distortion, and Growth: A Dynamic General Equilibrium Analysis with Altruistic Median Voter

detail.title: Aging, Political Distortion, and Growth: A Dynamic General Equilibrium Analysis with Altruistic Median Voter
detail.abstract: Population aging alters the political landscape, shifting fiscal policy toward redistribution and away from growth. This paper develops a dynamic overlapping generations model in which the tax rate and transfers are determined by the median voter. Unlike standard models, we assume older voters internalize future costs by caring about the utility of future generations. We show that aging still increases redistribution and reduces savings, but altruism mitigates political distortion relative to the purely selfish case. Compared to a Social Planner benchmark, majority voting remains inefficient, though the gap narrows as altruism rises. Our analysis provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the interaction between aging, politics, and growth, and highlights institutional and cultural factors that influence long-run outcomes.

title: Journal Review of “Microcontrollers Programming for and Automation in Undergraduate Biotechnology Engineering Education”
affiliations: Bulacan State University

detail.title: Journal Review of “Microcontrollers Programming for and Automation in Undergraduate Biotechnology Engineering Education”
detail.abstract: This review examines the article “Microcontrollers programming for control and automation in undergraduate biotechnology engineering education” by Márquez-Vera et al. (2023), which explores the integration of the ESP32 microcontroller into biotechnology engineering curricula. The study demonstrates how affordable, open-source tools can enhance student engagement, programming skills, and exposure to automation, artificial intelligence, and IoT applications. While the article’s strength lies in its accessibility and practical skill development, its limitation is the lack of discussion on scalability and industrial readiness. Overall, the review concludes that the ESP32 provides a valuable educational model for resource-limited institutions, with future research needed to assess its long-term impact on employability and industrial application.

title: Reclaiming Economics as a Moral Science: An Islamic Approach to Monetary Reform

detail.title: Reclaiming Economics as a Moral Science: An Islamic Approach to Monetary Reform

contentType.other: Accepted paper. To appear in Turkish Journal of Islamic Economics

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a new approach to monetary reform grounded in moral economy. Post-crisis reforms focus on technical fixes-macroprudential tools, regulatory redesign, and institutional safeguards-but ignore public welfare. Islamic finance has developed mechanisms for micro-level Shariah compliance but does not have institutional capabilities to protect the public interest. Bridging these gaps, the paper offers a triangular ethical architecture composed of three governance pillars: (i) banks as delegated creators of money; (ii) the state as regulator and macrocoordinator; and (iii) institutionalized moral authority, tasked with ensuring justice and public purpose in monetary governance. For the third pillar, we propose a Monetary Justice Commission, built to ensure just outcomes. The core claim is that financial systems built on public trust must serve public purpose, and that this requires enforceable ethical oversight. Using Pakistan as an illustrative case, the paper shows how moral authority can be embedded at the macro level to discipline monetary power under real-world conditions of institutional capture. The proposed architecture shifts monetary reform from technical engineering to normative governanceensuring that the power to create money is matched by a duty to protect the public good in both boom and bust.

title: Civil Rights and Self-Agency: A Critical Examination of Post-Movement African American Economic and Social Autonomy
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Civil Rights and Self-Agency: A Critical Examination of Post-Movement African American Economic and Social Autonomy
detail.abstract: This paper examines the complex legacy of the civil rights movement led by Martin Luther King Jr., specifically investigating whether the movement's emphasis on federal intervention and legal integration had unintended consequences for African American self-agency and community autonomy. While acknowledging the movement's essential role in dismantling Jim Crow and securing legal equality, this analysis explores empirical data regarding black economic institutions, family structures, and community self-determination in the pre-and post-civil rights eras. Drawing on historical economic data, sociological research, and King's own evolving economic thought, this paper argues that the civil rights movement's achievements must be understood alongside questions about the trade-offs between state-mediated equality and community-based selfsufficiency.

title: Trust in Resale Markets: A Simulation-based Study
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Trust in Resale Markets: A Simulation-based Study
detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a centralized resale mechanism designed to realign incentives and reduce market inefficiencies. The proposed system aims to:-

1. Establish seller credibility through platform-trusted verification mechanisms

2. Reduce information asymmetry by ensuring product descriptions and images are validated prior to listing

3. Lower transaction costs by integrating a door-to-door logistics network

4. Eliminate direct buyer-seller interaction, thereby preventing off-platform transactions and enforcing platform rules

The effectiveness of this mechanism is evaluated through a simulation-based model that compares market outcomes under the baseline and proposed systems.

title: Beyond Documentation: Governing Behavior, Environment, and Accountability in Healthcare

detail.title: Beyond Documentation: Governing Behavior, Environment, and Accountability in Healthcare

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Healthcare accountability frameworks disproportionately prioritize documentation review, outcome metrics, and retrospective investigation, while largely excluding the informal workplace behaviors, conversations, and environmental conditions that shape patient care in real time. Extensive patient safety research demonstrates that adverse events are rarely isolated; rather, they are preceded by observable cultural and behavioral indicators such as dismissive language, informal decision-making, power-based intimidation, and normalization of deviance. These precursors remain largely undocumented and ungoverned within existing healthcare oversight structures. Building on prior compliance-forward governance scholarship, including the Clinical Recording Compliance Auditor (CRCA), this paper proposes an Integrated Accountability Governance Division (IAGD): a multidisciplinary, preventive governance structure designed to oversee behavioral conduct, environmental treatment of patients and staff, and documentation integrity across healthcare settings. The model emphasizes transparency, restraint, workforce inclusion, and feasibility, reframing informal workplace behavior and communication as governable risk domains with direct implications for patient safety, equity, and institutional liability.

title: Punishing Crime, Ignoring Harm: Accountability Capture, Legal Design Failure, and Behavioral Enforcement Collapse in Healthcare

detail.title: Punishing Crime, Ignoring Harm: Accountability Capture, Legal Design Failure, and Behavioral Enforcement Collapse in Healthcare

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Despite extensive regulatory infrastructure, healthcare accountability in the United States remains largely inaccessible to patients who experience non-catastrophic but meaningful harm. Individuals harmed by delayed care, dismissive treatment, hostile clinical environments, or unprofessional conduct frequently encounter legal refusal, regulatory inaction, and institutional silence even when evidence exists. This paper argues that healthcare accountability systems are structurally designed to respond to criminality rather than harm, producing an enforcement gap that systematically excludes patients from remedy while protecting professional and institutional actors. Drawing on legal theory, malpractice scholarship, regulatory data, nursing discipline trends, patient safety research, and organizational governance literature, this paper introduces the concept of accountability capture, wherein selfregulating systems preserve institutional legitimacy at the expense of human impact. The analysis explains why attorneys avoid medical harm cases, why professional discipline centers on criminality rather than behavioral harm, and why safety-relevant conduct remains largely ungoverned despite clear patient safety implications. The paper concludes by proposing a Harm-Based Accountability Framework centered on behavioral enforcement, independent observation, and systematic measurement of risks that current systems fail to capture.

title: Interrogating the Nexus of Western Education and Religion for Entrepreneurship and Poverty Reduction: the Case of Nigeria
affiliations: The Polytechnic Ibadan - Department of Business Admin and Management Studies

detail.title: Interrogating the Nexus of Western Education and Religion for Entrepreneurship and Poverty Reduction: the Case of Nigeria
detail.abstract:
This study interrogates the nexus of education and religions (Christianity and Islam) in Nigeria and the extent to which it contributes to entrepreneurship and poverty reduction. To achieve this, three research questions are formulated and answered;
1.    Does religion affect the desire for western education?
2.    Does the acquisition of western education promote entrepreneurship?
3.    Does western education influence capacity for poverty reduction?
The study uses secondary data from across the 36 states of Nigeria including the Federal Capital Territory (FCT). Data analysis reveals that with between 80.9% and 87.8% killings in Nigeria in 2020-2022 traced to Islamic insurgency against western education in the North, scolionophobia (the fear of school) has set in, reducing desire for western education. With entrepreneurship included at almost all levels of western education, self-employment and decent paid employment, is promoted in the South that accepts it. Data analysis also reveals that income poverty in 2019 in the South is lower than the national average of 40.1% at 22.57%, which sharply contrasts with 59.76% of the North that antagonises western education. Data on 2022 Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) affirms the same position. For the South, the MPI of 0.195 is lower than the national figure of 0.257, implying that South with its western education reduces both income poverty and multidimensional poverty better. This Chapter argues that the nexus of western education and Christianity which has played a strong role in poverty reduction and entrepreneurship in Nigeria’s South is needed in the country’s North, that is characterised by  high poverty and business mortality rates. Appropriate recommendations are made to achieve this.

title: When AI Teaches Economics: How Dataset Constraints and Prompts Shape Pedagogical Quality
affiliations: and Franklin and Marshall College

detail.title: When AI Teaches Economics: How Dataset Constraints and Prompts Shape Pedagogical Quality

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study as it utilizes exclusively de-identified, publicly available secondary data.

detail.abstract: The present paper investigates the effectiveness of generative artificial intelligence as a learning tool for undergraduate microeconomics students. The study implements an experimental design that compares a constrained condition, in which an AI is limited to a microeconomics textbook, with an unconstrained condition, in which the same system can draw on its full training corpus and the web for both quantitative and qualitative content. Using OpenAI’s ChatGPT 5.1 with carefully engineered prompts, this study examines AI explanations of the Coase theorem and the relationship between monopoly and externalities along three academic learning points: accuracy, pedagogical scaffolding, and vulnerability to hallucination and logical inconsistency. The results reveal an asymmetric pattern. In the quantitative unconstrained condition, the AI provides rich numerical examples and step-by-step reasoning that are well-suited to building quantitative intuition, but it also introduces conceptual oversimplifications and occasional logical tension when pressured with edge case questions. Instead, the study argues that generative AI should supplement, rather than replace, textbooks as the primary foundation for economic frameworks, and that its value depends critically on students’ capacity to read AI-generated explanations with the same critical literacy they apply to formal course materials.

title: The Double-Edged Sword: Unveiling the Impact of Women's Financial Inclusion on Intimate Partner Violence in India
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology, Hyderabad, Shiv Nadar University and Indian Institute of Technology Hyderabad

detail.title: The Double-Edged Sword: Unveiling the Impact of Women's Financial Inclusion on Intimate Partner Violence in India
detail.abstract: We empirically examine the causal impact of women's financial inclusion on their exposure to Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) using data from the fifth round of the National Family Health Survey (NFHS), India. However, establishing a causal link between women's financial inclusion and IPV is challenging due to unobserved confounders and reverse causality. To overcome these obstacles, we adopt a nonparametric bounds approach. Relying on relatively weak assumptions, we find robust evidence that women's financial inclusion significantly increases their exposure to IPV. Further, we provide suggestive evidence that this result arises because women's financial inclusion is likely to disrupt patriarchal beliefs about gender roles, lead to female guilt, and increase husbands' use of IPV for instrumental reasons. Our findings suggest that empowering women financially, while crucial, may inadvertently increase their vulnerability to IPV unless such initiatives are paired with efforts to shift underlying cultural norms surrounding gender.

title: Graphical Information and Inflation Expectations: Evidence from Japan
affiliations: Yokohama City University

detail.title: Graphical Information and Inflation Expectations: Evidence from Japan
detail.abstract:
This paper examines how central bank communication shapes household inflation expectations, using evidence from two randomized controlled trials conducted in Japan. The first experiment presents households with graphical highlights from the Bank of Japan's Outlook for Economic Activity and Prices, including information on the macroeconomic outlook, yield curve control, and official inflation forecasts. The second experiment isolates the role of communication format by comparing the effects of graphical, narrative, and technical-text presentations of identical inflation-related content. 
Across both experiments, exposure to central bank information significantly reduces oneyear-ahead inflation expectations. The effects are strongest for policy-relevant and quantitative information, such as yield curve control and inflation forecasts. Belief revisions are heterogeneous and consistent with Bayesian updating: individuals with higher prior expectations revise their beliefs more strongly, and more comprehensible formats lead to more precise posterior beliefs. While simplified text formats generate larger average downward revisions, graphical formats are particularly effective in reducing the dispersion of beliefs. 
These findings highlight that not only the content but also the presentation of central bank communication plays a crucial role in shaping household expectations. Well-designed, accessible communication can enhance policy transmission by improving both the level and precision of inflation expectations.

title: A Review of on the Regulation of Currencies (1844) by John Fullarton (Esq) ¶

detail.title: A Review of on the Regulation of Currencies (1844) by John Fullarton (Esq) ¶

detail.abstract: This paper reviews On the Regulation of Currencies (1844) by John Fullarton (Esq). It is a companion to The Life and Times of John Fullarton (Esq) (1778-1849): A Documentary Reassessment, which provides biographical context for Fullarton's monetary views. The paper examines Fullarton's critique of Britain's banking system and the Bank Charter Act 1844, in which he argued that banknote issuance should be constrained by metallic backing under gold and silver standards. Although written in the mid-nineteenth century, the work remains a significant contribution to debates on currency regulation and monetary stability. The paper further considers the relevance of Fullarton's arguments by reference to Australia's transition from a gold-backed currency adopted in 1911 to a floating exchange rate regime in 1983.

title: HPQKX: A Hybrid Post-Quantum Key Exchange Protocol with Temporal Binding for Financial Applications

detail.title: HPQKX: A Hybrid Post-Quantum Key Exchange Protocol with Temporal Binding for Financial Applications
detail.abstract: The imminent threat of quantum computing to current cryptographic infrastructure necessitates the development of practical post-quantum secure protocols, particularly for financial technology applications where both security and performance are critical. We present HPQKX (Hybrid Post-Quantum Key Exchange), a novel cryptographic protocol that combines Ring-Learning With Errors (Ring-LWE) lattice-based cryptography with hash-based temporal binding and classical elliptic curve cryptography to provide defense-in-depth security against both classical and quantum adversaries. Our protocol introduces an innovative Merkle tree-based temporal binding mechanism that provides forward secrecy with sub-microsecond update overhead while maintaining resistance to replay attacks. Through comprehensive optimization including Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) acceleration, SIMD vectorization, and adaptive security parameters, HPQKX achieves a complete key exchange in approximately 85 microseconds on modern hardware, a 10× improvement over naïve implementations while providing 128-bit post-quantum security. We provide formal security proofs under the Ring-LWE assumption and the Random Oracle Model, demonstrate practical implementation efficiency across diverse platforms (desktop, mobile, IoT), and evaluate the protocol’s applicability to real-world financial systems including blockchain consensus, cross-border payment authentication, and secure API communications. Our results indicate that post-quantum security is achievable without sacrificing the performance requirements of modern financial infrastructure.

title: Covariance Implied Risk Factors
affiliations: Insper Institute of Education and Research

detail.title: Covariance Implied Risk Factors
detail.abstract: This paper examines the role of heteroskedasticity in extracting latent risk factors from asset returns. I show that standard principal component analysis suffers from distortions when assets exhibit heterogeneous idiosyncratic variances, leading factors to reflect clusters of idiosyncratic risk rather than true systematic risk. Building on recent developments in the statistics literature, I apply heteroskedastic PCA (heteroPCA) to correct for this bias by iteratively replacing the diagonal of the sample covariance matrix with estimates implied by the off-diagonal structure. This approach delivers superior out-of-sample cross-sectional pricing performance compared to standard PCA, with higher Sharpe ratios and lower average pricing errors across multiple equity portfolios. The identified factors exhibit clear economic interpretability, and the implied stochastic discount factor achieves lower Hansen-Jagannathan distances. These results highlight that accounting for heteroskedasticity in idiosyncratic variance substantially improves factor estimation in asset pricing applications.

title: Scaling Generative AI: Diminishing Marginal Returns and Firm-Level Outcomes
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank and Deutsche Bundesbank - Economics Department

detail.title: Scaling Generative AI: Diminishing Marginal Returns and Firm-Level Outcomes
detail.abstract: Using the Bundesbank Online Panel-Firms (BOP-F) survey of over 7,000 German manufacturing and services firms (Q2 2025), this paper provides rare firm-level evidence on generative AI (GenAI) diffusion, costs, and expected economic effects. Diffusion is rapid on the extensive margin, while intensive use deepens more gradually as adopters scale applications over time and new users start small. GenAI-related expenses are already economically meaningful, and reported spending is expected to rise markedly from 2024 to 2026. Within a given year, higher spending is associated with higher usage intensity but diminishing marginal gains. Firms' expectations are strongly positive for productivity, imply rising high-skill demand, little change in low-skill employment, and gradually rising wages.

title: Assigning a Treatment under Hidden Spillovers

detail.title: Assigning a Treatment under Hidden Spillovers

detail.abstract: This paper studies the assignment of a treatment by a social planner when the valuations of the treatment are interdependent across individuals in the population. Specifically, an individual's valuation of the treatment is influenced by the treatment status of some group of individuals and is positive if and only if any member of the group is treated. The identities of those who have positive spillovers on an individual is his private type, and the social planner assigns the treatment based on their reported types aiming to maximize the number of treated individuals less subsidies. We study the property of an assignment mechanism that offers a subsidy to a single individual and provides the treatment to everyone over whom this individual has positive spillovers either directly or indirectly. We use the percolation theorem of McDiarmid (1981) to show that the number of treated individuals under such a mechanism is independent of the reciprocal property of the spillover relationship, and is asymptotically optimal when the population grows large.

title: Role of Pharmacists in Generic Pharmaceutical Adoption
affiliations: University of Wisconsin - Madison, Department of Economics, Students and Keio University

detail.title: Role of Pharmacists in Generic Pharmaceutical Adoption
detail.abstract: This study examines how pharmacists shape consumers' brand preferences in the Japanese generic drug market. Prior research has shown that consumers are generally willing to pay for brand-name products. However, we note a puzzle: even when a brand-identical authorized generic (AG) is available and priced the same as an ordinary generic (OG), many patients still choose to receive the OGs. We develop a model that jointly characterizes patients' demands for drugs and pharmacies' endogenous adoption of AGs versus OGs, then estimate the model using panel data on pharmacy-level dispensing outcomes and adoption histories. The model estimates indicate heterogeneity in brand preference across pharmacies that is linked to the qualifications of the pharmacists, especially those who serve as family pharmacists. The results also show that counseling-guided, context-dependent brand preferences help explain demand for OGs.

title: Developing a Framework for Improved Data Use in Health Management at the District Level in Malawi Health Management Information System
affiliations: University of Malawi, University of Malawi and University of Oslo

detail.title: Developing a Framework for Improved Data Use in Health Management at the District Level in Malawi Health Management Information System
detail.abstract: The effective use of Health Management Information Systems (HMIS) is critical for strengthening decision-making and resource allocation in healthcare, particularly in low and middle-income countries such as Malawi. Yet, district level data use remains constrained by institutional challenges that undermine the potential of HMIS. This study proposes a framework to enhance data use in health management at the district level, drawing on institutional theory and the dynamics of coercive, normative and mimetic pressures. A qualitative approach was employed, including semi-structured interviews, participant observations, and documents analysis, to examine how these pressures shape data practices within Malawi’s health sector. Findings reveal that improved data use depends on key activities such as regulating practices, building human capacity, sustaining efforts, integrating data tools and platforms, coordinating processes and partnerships, motivating contributions, and sharing best practices. By addressing these institutional concerns, the proposed framework offers actionable recommendations for policymakers and practitioners to foster a culture of data use, strengthen health management decision-making, and advance ICT4D scholarship on HMIS effectiveness and health outcomes in low and middle-income settings.

title: Coffee shop menu calorie labelling: effects on beliefs, knowledge and behaviour and the role of food choice motives
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Liverpool and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Coffee shop menu calorie labelling: effects on beliefs, knowledge and behaviour and the role of food choice motives
detail.abstract: Calorie labelling has been implemented as a public health strategy to address obesity, but its mechanisms of action are not well understood. Drawing on expectancy-value models, this study explored whether calorie labelling influences the calorie content of items selected from a hypothetical coffee shop menu via changes in outcome expectancies and whether effects are moderated by food choice motives. Adults (n = 577) were randomly assigned to view a menu with or without calorie information and choose from the menu. Participants rated outcome expectancies (weight control, health, taste, value for money and fullness) for each menu item before and after viewing the menu and completed measures of weight control, health, price and sensory appeal motivation using the Food Choice Questionnaire (FCQ). Participants also estimated calories for each item. Labelling did not significantly reduce calories selected (p = .18), though means were in the predicted direction (labelling M = 371, SD = 261; no labelling M = 392, SD = 249, 5% decrease). Labelling significantly increased health, weight control and value for money expectations of menu items but these changes did not influence calories selected. A sensitivity analysis suggested moderation by weight control motivation whereby labelling reduced calories selected among highly motivated participants, although this effect was not observed across other models. Exploratory analyses showed that labelling also improved calorie estimation accuracy. Findings suggest that while calorie labelling may influence beliefs and knowledge, its acute impact on population level behaviour may be minimal.

title: Higher Order Income Risk and the Business Cycle: Evidence From the Netherlands
affiliations: Tilburg University - Department of Finance and Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Department of Business Economics

detail.title: Higher Order Income Risk and the Business Cycle: Evidence From the Netherlands
detail.abstract: Using population administrative data for the Netherlands (1999-2022), we study time-series and cross-sectional variation in earnings levels and growth. Earnings inequality dynamics differ sharply by gender: men see a widening from 1999 to 2015 driven by declines at the bottom, while women exhibit lower-tail compression, partly linked to hours worked, and strong gains at the top. We also estimate the business-cycle exposure of the full earnings growth distribution by extending the standard beta approach to quantile betas: We estimate the sensitivity of different quantiles to variations in GDP growth and map our estimates into quantile-based dispersion (P90-P10), Kelley's skewness, and Crow-Siddiqui kurtosis measures by gender, age, and permanentincome (PI) rank. Skewness is strongly procyclical and it is the main driver of countercyclical income risk. Business-cycle sensitivity is a tail phenomenon: medians are nearly acyclical, whereas the 10th and 90th percentiles are strongly procyclical, especially at the bottom and at the top of the PI distribution. Consistently, tail movements explain most cyclical variation in mean earnings growth (mean betas).

title: Physiological determinants of water-use efficiency,  biomass, and yield in spring wheat are growth-stage dependent as revealed by UAV vegetation indices
affiliations: University of Alberta, University of Alberta, University of Saskatchewan, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Alberta, University of Alberta and University of Alberta

detail.title: Physiological determinants of water-use efficiency,  biomass, and yield in spring wheat are growth-stage dependent as revealed by UAV vegetation indices
detail.abstract: Vegetation indices (VIs) derived from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery are widely used in crop phenotyping; however, their ability to discriminate cultivars under field conditions is often constrained by strong environmental and phenological effects. This study quantified the relative contributions of environment, growth stage, and cultivar to variation in spectral VIs associated with grain yield, biomass, and water-use efficiency (WUE) in spring wheat. Growth stage and year were the dominant sources of variation across yield, biomass, and nearly all VIs, indicating that canopy spectral responses are primarily controlled by developmental dynamics and seasonal variability. Growth stage exhibited exceptionally high F-values, reflecting strong physiological transitions in chlorophyll content, canopy structure, and senescence, as captured by vegetation indices from booting through maturity. Environmental effects strongly influenced canopy reflectance and productivity. Cultivar effects were modest and largely confined to physiologically targeted vegetation indices, with IKAW and ExRv2 showing the strongest and most consistent discriminatory capacity, while CIred-edge, RECI, NDREI, RDVI, and GNDVIv2 provided weaker and less stable varietal differentiation. Widely used broad-spectrum greenness indices such as NDVI, ExG, RGBVI, VARI, and RVI exhibited saturation and limited physiological specificity, constraining their utility for reliable cultivar discrimination under field conditions. Stage-specific correlation analyses further revealed strong phenological dependence of VI relevance. At booting, red-edge dynamics along with chlorophyll-sensitive indices were positively associated with yield, biomass, and water-use efficiency, identifying this stage as optimal for early indirect selection. At heading, VIs mainly reflected canopy stability and stress sensitivity, whereas at maturity, spectral responses were dominated by senescence with minimal predictive value. Effective phenotyping in wheat using UAV relies on growth-stage normalization and red-edge–based, physiologically informed indices for modern breeding programs. Effective phenotyping in wheat using UAV therefore requires growth-stage normalization and physiologically informed, red-edge–based indices for modern breeding.

title: Well-informed choices? Effects of information interventions in primary care on care quality
affiliations: Lund University, VIVE - The Danish Center for Social Science Research, Lund University and University of Gothenburg

detail.title: Well-informed choices? Effects of information interventions in primary care on care quality
detail.abstract: Market frictions, such as imperfect information or hassle costs, may reduce the efficiency of consumer choice in healthcare settings. We use data from two randomised policy interventions in a Swedish region, which improved the access to information about primary care providers and reduced the switching costs of one percent of the adult population and of a sample of new residents. We examine the intervention effects on a large number of clinical process quality measures, access to care, and adverse health events, measured at the individual level. We find no significant effect of the interventions on any of the outcomes.

title: Khan K-Vol: A Normalised Kurtosis Adjusted Volatility Estimator
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Khan K-Vol: A Normalised Kurtosis Adjusted Volatility Estimator
detail.abstract:
In this technical note, we develop the Khan Kurtosis Adjusted Volatility Estimator (Khan K-Vol) to supersede the use of Standard Deviation as a parametric estimator within Normal Distribution applications, with a Normalised Kurtosis Adjusted Standard Deviation. Instead of changing the distribution to fit the empirical sample, we change the volatility to fit a wider Normal Distribution that reflects the estimate of Kurtosis within a new Standard Deviation estimator, K-Vol.

Succinctly: the Khan K-Vol Kurtosis Adjusted Volatility Estimator equals the parametric Standard Deviation estimate multiplied by the fourth root of the ratio of the parametric Kurtosis estimate divided by the Normalised Kurtosis parametric value of 3. Kurtosis Adjusted Volatility K-Vol = StandardDeviation * (Kurtosis/3)^1/4

The K-Vol estimator lends itself well to extreme value analysis, in particular Value at Risk analysis, by simply replacing the parametric estimate of Standard Deviation with K-Vol, such that KVaR (1-p) = the Normal Standard Deviation Z-Score of p times K-Vol. So for example, the KVaR99.5 equals the Z-Score 2.6 times K-Vol.

We perform an empirical analysis over 20 years of out-of-sample daily backtesting to ascertain the the KVaR99.5 estimator works well for all asset classes, on par with empirical distributions such as HVaR. Given that many empirical distributions are simulations-based in practice, we make the recommendation to perform the simulations with K-Vol as the volatility estimator and parameter.

Next we derive an autocorrelation function for a rolling window with an autocorrelation equal to the ratio of t-k over t, where t is the rolling window and k is the step-ahead, and then we derive the concomitant required sample size with autocorrelation as a Tau factor equal to the ratio of 1 over 1 minus the autocorrelation factor, which for Basel FRTB equals a Tau factor of 10 on the data sample. Thus, in order to address the impractical sample size requirements for the tasks of backtesting risk distributions, we make the suggestion that K-Vol can be used for simulations in order to satisfy the Tau factor requirements on data size in the presence of the autocorrelation implicit in rolling statistics.

Finally, we use K-Vol to analyse the Implied Volatility in options prices to determine whether K-Vol has explanatory power in reconciling the observed empirical discrepancy of the Volatility Risk Premium. We look at the model-free VIX as a proxy for the Implied Volatility of the SP500 and compare this to K-Vol, and we ascertain over 30 years of out-of-sample daily data that we can achieve the same level as the VIX, hence explaining the Volatility Risk Premium in terms of Kurtosis. We review one possible theory behind the efficacy of the K-Vol estimator from viewing Kurtosis as being a good estimator for what we term Oura (pronounced "aura", the volatility of log volatility).

title: Watzlawick in the Infosphere: Meaning, Paradox, and the Algorithmic Construction of Reality
affiliations: CNR - Intitute for Complex Systems

detail.title: Watzlawick in the Infosphere: Meaning, Paradox, and the Algorithmic Construction of Reality
detail.abstract:
Paul Watzlawick argued that reality is not discovered but constructed through communication. This paper extends his radical constructivist framework to the digital age, tracing how information technologies have progressively automated the construction of what Watzlawick called "second-order reality" - the domain of meaning, value, and significance.

The analysis follows three technological regimes. Search engines transferred epistemic authority from human judgment to algorithmic ranking, making relevance a function of network topology rather than truth. Social media fragmented shared reality into parallel epistemic bubbles, where narrative resonance supplants factual accuracy. Large Language Models complete this trajectory: they produce fluent, coherent discourse without comprehension, intention, or reference - making "hallucination" not a malfunction but the default mode of a system that generates meaning without anchoring it to anything beyond statistical probability.

The paper introduces the concept of algorithmic constructivism to characterize this new condition, and warns of its anthropological consequence: epistemic atrophy. As sense-making is progressively delegated to automated systems, humans risk losing the capacity to distinguish negotiated meaning from algorithmic simulation - and with it, the ability to construct reality through genuine communicative exchange.

title: War Reindustrialization of Europe: Defense Industrial Complexes As Pillars of Strategic Autonomy

detail.title: War Reindustrialization of Europe: Defense Industrial Complexes As Pillars of Strategic Autonomy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal for Strategy, Technology and Defense Sciences | 2025, #4, p. 9-27

detail.abstract: The article explores the phenomenon of Europe's war reindustrialization after 2022 as a strategic response to altered security dynamics due to rising eastern threats. The aim is to provide empirical insight into this transformation and develop a conceptual framework for understanding its long-term implications. We analyze the military-industrial complex as a multidimensional security, economic, high-tech, and social phenomenon. We examine three hypotheses: (1) war reindustrialization is not merely a short-term reaction but a long-term strategic reorientation, (2) the process dynamics show significant variations conditioned by geographical position, historical experiences, and economic capacities, and (3) the revitalized military-industrial complex creates a new economic reality that alters power relations within the EU and NATO. Methodologically, we apply a mixed approach: quantitative analysis of military budgets, comparative analysis of strategies, and case studies. Results show a 32% increase in NATO members military budgets (2021-2023), opening of 70+ new facilities, creation of 210,000 jobs, and high correlation (r=0.78) between geographical proximity to threats and intensity of reindustrialization. We conclude that war reindustrialization represents a fundamental paradigm shift that will shape the security architecture, economic structure, and geopolitical position of the continent in the coming decades.

title: Hearing The Prophet: Two American Composers and the First Musical Life of Orphalese

detail.title: Hearing The Prophet: Two American Composers and the First Musical Life of Orphalese

publicationDetails.detailsText: Hourani, G. G. (2026, January 15). Hearing The Prophet: Two American Composers and the First Musical Life of Orphalese. Echoes Logos, V.2, No. 1. https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31073023.

detail.abstract:
This essay uncovers a forgotten chapter in the afterlife of Kahlil Gibran’s The Prophet. Drawing on archival recordings, musical scores, and concert histories, it examines how two American composers—Gardner Read and Minuetta Kessler—produced what appear to be the earliest known musical settings of The Prophet in the United States, and possibly worldwide. Their compositions represent the first sustained attempts to give Gibran’s text a musical voice.

The essay argues that through these works, The Prophet moved beyond its condition as a literary text shaped by displacement and circulation and entered the realm of American devotional music. Balancing monumentality and intimacy, the musical settings transformed the book into something to be returned to, listened within, and dwelt in.

By tracing this overlooked sonic afterlife, the essay explores how music enabled The Prophet to acquire a second life in sound, reconfiguring its reception and opening new questions about memory, belonging, and cultural location.

title: Geometric Properties of Continuous-Time Inflation in Energy Markets
affiliations: Environmental Protection Program

detail.title: Geometric Properties of Continuous-Time Inflation in Energy Markets
detail.abstract: We propose a continuous-time definition of inflation for energy markets, in which inflation is treated as a local geometric property of the price process rather than as a weighted average of price levels. Inflation is defined as the logarithmic time derivative I r (t) of a normalized cost function, with the associated discounting function D(t) encoding the structural dynamics of valuation. Using daily data from the TGE BASE index (December 2025), we analyze the effects of linear and cubic spline interpolation on the inferred inflation dynamics and discounting structure. We introduce two original stability measures-the Amplitude Stability Index (BSI) and the Temporal Stability Coefficient (T SC)-which characterize the balance and temporal symmetry of inflationary and deflationary regimes. The results reveal a high degree of structural invariance of the discounting function with respect to shifts in the valuation baseline, indicating that the energy market operates as a quasi-stable oscillatory system. This framework provides a geometric alternative to average-based inflation measures and offers a continuous-time perspective on market stability.

title: "Reciprocal Tariffs" as a Geoeconomic Policy Tool: Insights from Southeast Asia

detail.title: "Reciprocal Tariffs" as a Geoeconomic Policy Tool: Insights from Southeast Asia
detail.abstract: This article provides novel insights into the political economy of President Trump's use of "reciprocal tariffs" with empirical evidence from Southeast Asia-a region at the centre of the U.S.-China power rivalry. For the first time, all Southeast Asian countries face simultaneous threats of unprecedentedly high tariff rates, offering a unique case for analysis. The article contributes to the growing literature on geoeconomic policy instruments by examining five aspects: (i) the nature and the deployment of tariffs in the contemporary era of U.S. protectionism; (ii) domestic political determinants of the origin-based tariff rate decision; (iii) how asymmetries in bargaining power limit the tariff negotiating capacity of smaller states visà-vis hegemons; (iv) the implications of divergent national interests, regional disputes and conflicts, and international competition for Southeast Asian regional cohesion; and (v) the hedging strategy or bamboo diplomacy of Southeast Asian countries as an instructive model for other small states navigating geoeconomic pressures.

detail.abstract: This note examines the pricing eciency of rough volatility options models against the Black-Scholes benchmark in high-beta technology equities (NVDA, TSLA) during the 20252026 volatility regime. Using Hairer's regularity structures to calibrate a rough Hurst exponent (H < 0.15), the study nds that rough path "lifting" signicantly outperforms Ito-semimartingale models. Empirical results demonstrate a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) improvement of over 95% for Out-of-the-Money options. These ndings suggest that "roughness" is a structural feature of modern tech liquidity clusters, rendering standard diusion-based models inadequate for tail-risk management.

title: Transmission of MBS Credit Risk to Mortgage Rate Disparity

detail.title: Transmission of MBS Credit Risk to Mortgage Rate Disparity
detail.abstract: This paper shows that MBS market credit risk introduces fluctuation in mortgage rate disparity between high-and low-income applicants in the U.S. The MBS credit risk drop incentivizes MBS investors to provide credit liquidity to mortgage market, resulting in a distorted disparity in mortgage rate across applicants' income spectrum. Mortgage market liquidity originating outside the MBS credit risk dynamics cannot account for this disparity. Quantitative easings are employed as policy shocks to strengthen the causal identification. This disparity emerges through the demand channel, where high-income applicants respond to improved MBS liquidity by expanding their borrowing activity.

title: The Implications of Using Aggregate Price Index Data When Testing Purchasing Power Parity for Flexible-Price Monetary Approach Exchange Rate Models

detail.title: The Implications of Using Aggregate Price Index Data When Testing Purchasing Power Parity for Flexible-Price Monetary Approach Exchange Rate Models

declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethics approval was required for this paper.

detail.abstract: Crownover et al. (1996) suggested that the literature applying unit root, stationarity and cointegration tests of long-run purchasing power parity (PPP) with price index data test relative PPP and not absolute PPP. Regarding this contention we argue the following. First, the traditional relative PPP specification, that implies a relationship between the logarithms of the exchange rate and (relative) prices in difference form, is not being tested. Rather the form of relative PPP being tested is a relationship between the levels of these variables. Second, because exchange rate indices are rarely used in empirical PPP tests this implies that the base period of the exchange rate is restricted to unity in the levels relative PPP specification that is typically tested in the literature. Third, this restricted levels relative PPP specification is observationally equivalent to the strong form of absolute PPP that allows for constant transportation costs and other constant barriers to trade. We further show that support for this restricted levels relative PPP specification (unlike traditional relative PPP in differences) remains useful in terms of establishing a modified long-run flexible-price monetary approach (FLMA) exchange rate model in levels. We also demonstrate that even when the proportionality and/or symmetry conditions do not hold in a log-levels PPP specification, provided there is an equilibrium relation they still usefully imply modified versions of the long-run FLMA exchange rate model in levels.

title: Reducing Frictions while Shopping In-Store - The Effect of using a Mobile App Scan & Go Technology on Consumer Purchasing Behavior

detail.title: Reducing Frictions while Shopping In-Store - The Effect of using a Mobile App Scan & Go Technology on Consumer Purchasing Behavior

declarations.funderStatement: This study has been partially supported by the Dutch Research Council (NWO) via grant 406.21.EB.010.

detail.abstract: Self-service technologies (SSTs) that replace regular checkout are widely deployed in grocery retailing to reduce customer frictions and labor needs, yet their impact on consumer purchasing behavior remains unclear. We study a specific type of these SSTs: mobile app 'scan & go' technologies. Mobile app scan & go technologies may lower customer time and effort spent during a shopping trip by eliminating queuing and double handling. However, they also shift scanning effort to customers, which may change attention and shopping patterns. We explore how customers adopt mobile app scan & go technologies in practice, and study the causal effect of adoption on their purchasing behavior. We partner with a European grocery retailer that introduced a mobile app scan & go technology in their physical stores and analyze a large transactional dataset spanning more than 7 million purchases from nearly 60,000 customers. Leveraging the staggered adoption timing and matched non-adopters, we estimate the effect of adoption using difference-in-differences designs with customer and time fixed effects and modern staggered-DiD estimators. We find that adoption increases customers' monthly purchase frequency and total monthly spending, with little change in average basket value. We also find that adoption is not 'all-or-nothing': most adopters use the scan & go technology selectively for particular shopping trips, and about one-third try it once and then discontinue using it. The observed spending and frequency gains are concentrated among customers who use the technology repeatedly. These findings suggest that mobile app scan & go technologies can strengthen customer retention, but only when they reliably reduce customer friction. Retailers should promote mobile app scan & go usage for 'major' grocery trips and design onboarding and in-store support to reduce first-use learning costs - because repeated usage, not mere adoption, is what drives performance benefits.

title: How Responsive Design Can Foster Responsible Innovation
affiliations: Center for Creative Foresight and Wolf Stake Consulting LLC

detail.title: How Responsive Design Can Foster Responsible Innovation
detail.abstract: This article explores how businesses can draw inspiration from responsive behaviors of living systems, such as self-assembly, self-cleaning, self-healing, thermoregulation, responsive motion, active coloration, and plasticity, to design products and solutions that exemplify responsible innovation. In a business environment where both customer focus and social demands are paramount concerns for companies, responsible innovation requires the creation of products and solutions that balance the incentives and interests of various internal and external stakeholders. The article highlights how living organisms provide valuable insights into fostering responsible innovation, as they are adept at maintaining a delicate equilibrium between their well-being and their impact on the environment. This equilibrium is achieved through various responsive behaviors that form the basis of "responsive design," involving emulating nature to create products with similar responsive characteristics.

title: How Robot Adoption Impacts Stock Market Outcomes
affiliations: University of Colorado at Denver - Department of Finance

detail.title: How Robot Adoption Impacts Stock Market Outcomes
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of robotics, accelerated by advances in artificial intelligence, is reshaping economic activity and financial markets. This paper examines how robot adoption influences stock market outcomes, focusing on returns and volatility. We assemble a novel crosscountry dataset from the International Federation of Robotics (IFR) that disaggregates robot revenues into industrial and service components. We document a robust positive relationship between industrial robot revenue and stock market returns, consistent with automation-driven productivity gains being capitalized into equity prices. To address endogeneity concerns, we employ an instrumental-variable approach based on a Bartik-style exposure framework. Our central mechanism hypothesis posits that robots raise labor productivity, measured as output per worker, which in turn enhances market performance. In contrast, service robot revenue is associated with higher stock market volatility, reflecting increased uncertainty surrounding service-sector automation. A comprehensive set of robustness tests, including alternative panel specifications and controls for country political institutions, confirms the stability of our results. Overall, the findings highlight the heterogeneous and economically meaningful effects of robotics on global financial markets.

title: Gaps and opportunities in climate adaptation planning across South American cities: a systematic analysis of local plans
