detail.title: Gaps and opportunities in climate adaptation planning across South American cities: a systematic analysis of local plans
detail.abstract: Urban areas in the Global South are highly vulnerable to natural hazards, yet they are underrepresented in research monitoring climate adaptation efforts. To address this gap, we analyse 64 local adaptation plans from 37 cities with over one million inhabitants to assess how adaptation is being planned in South America and the role of nature-based solutions (NbS). Results show that plans tend to emphasise educational, informational, and behavioural measures, whereas engineering and technological approaches are least prioritised. The types of measures vary by hazard: NbS are the preferred options for adapting to floods and heatwaves, whereas engineering and technological approaches are preferred for droughts. National adaptation plans were found to play a key role in shaping local priorities, either enabling or constraining the adoption of NbS. The findings reveal key gaps in adaptation planning, particularly in relation to public health and risk-transfer measures, which are hardly considered. As such, our findings provide policymakers, planners, donors, and researchers with valuable insights for improving urban climate resilience in South America.

detail.abstract: This research examines the role of peer reviews on consumer demand for a set of competing products within a well-defined category. We developed and distributed a survey to collect data on consumers' willingness to pay (WTP) for sparkling wines from France, Spain, and the United States under different information treatments. detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of working from home (WFH) on firm-level outcomes. It uses detailed survey, balance sheet and matched employer-employee data on Italian firms from before the pandemic and up to 2023. For some firms, whose labour productivity did not decline, the pandemic-induced shift to WFH was maintained after the emergency ended.

detail.title:
A Machine Learning Framework to Explain Variance and Forecast Performance in Google Search Ads 
Driver Attribution for Wins and Cost Per Win (CPW) Using Random Forest (R²) and Gradient Boosting (MAPE)
detail.abstract: DAT Freight & Analytics operates one of the largest freight marketplaces in North America, connecting carriers with available loads through its load board subscription SaaS platform. Carriers typically purchase access through a self-serve, self-sign-up process on the DAT website, making Google Search Ads a primary demand-capture channel. Within this measurement framework, a completed carrier subscription checkout is recorded as a Win, and the advertising cost required to generate one completed checkout is defined as Cost Per Win (CPW). This acquisition motion resembles an eCommerce-style funnel: prospects discover DAT through high-intent search queries, evaluate the offering quickly, and convert through an online checkout or subscription workflow with minimal sales involvement. Google Search Ads performance in this environment is influenced by demand shifts in freight markets, auction competition, keyword intent mix, ad relevance, and bidding constraints. While dashboards describe what happened, they often fail to quantify why performance moved and how reliably the next period can be predicted. This paper introduces a practical two-stage machine learning framework designed specifically for Google Search Ads reporting data supporting DAT's carrier subscription growth. The framework combines: 1. Variance explanation using Random Forest feature importance with interpretability measured by R² 2. Strategic forecasting using Gradient Boosting time-series regression with accuracy measured by MAPE Using daily campaign performance metrics aggregated into monthly outcomes, this approach explains the key drivers of Wins and Cost Per Win (CPW) and produces a forward-looking forecast for quarterly planning. detail.abstract: Design amplification is a process whereby innovations originally created for users with disabilities are expanded to unlock universal market value. Drawing on an in-depth study of LIXIL and over 150 archival examples, this Harvard Business Review article identifies four levels of amplification: marginalized users, other marginalized groups, situational users, and mainstream consumers. The authors present a five-step Design Amplification Playbook: (1) selecting a focal disability, (2) mapping the user journey, (3) identifying cross-segment benefits, (4) designing for scalability, and (5) validating across all segments.

detail.abstract: Over the past two decades, marketing automation has evolved from simple tools for campaign management into a sophisticated ecosystem powered by AI, big data, and predictive analytics. This transformation enables firms to manage omnichannel campaigns, personalize content at scale, and optimize decision-making in real time, shifting marketing from intuition-based practices to data-driven strategies. Beyond operational efficiency, marketing automation acts as a strategic resource that reshapes customer relationships, competitive dynamics, and organizational performance. Its implementation requires significant organizational changes, including crossfunctional collaboration, new capabilities in data literacy and algorithmic thinking, and the emergence of hybrid roles that integrate marketing and technology expertise. Human implications are equally profound, as routine tasks become automated and marketers assume roles emphasizing creativity, strategy, and ethical judgment, raising concerns about skill displacement and workforce polarization. Additionally, marketing automation introduces ethical, social, and governance challenges, including data privacy, algorithmic bias, and accountability. Firms must balance innovation with transparency, trust, and responsible use of AI to maintain customer confidence. This study highlights the multidimensional impact of marketing automation, emphasizing the need for integrated research that considers strategic, organizational, human, and ethical perspectives in shaping its future trajectory.

title: LLM Adoption and Legacy Translators in Korea: Evidence on Engagement, Exploration, and Reallocation
affiliations: Korea Information Society Development Institute (KISDI) and

detail.title: LLM Adoption and Legacy Translators in Korea: Evidence on Engagement, Exploration, and Reallocation
detail.abstract: This study examines how adoption of a large language model (LLM) reshapes usage of incumbent online translation services in an Asian market. Using weekly app and web usage logs from Korea, this study quantifies how the adoption of ChatGPT changes legacy-translator engagement, brand exploration, and within-portfolio reallocation. First, legacy engagement increases after adoption and remains statistically detectable for roughly 15 to 17 weeks, then attenuates and is at times indistinguishable from zero thereafter. Second, brand diversity widens only at onboarding, consistent with short-run exploration rather than durable multihoming. Third, reallocation is brand specific: prior Google users shift time away from Google, prior Bing users diversify into Papago while maintaining Bing, and prior Papago users further concentrate on Papago. Heterogeneity analyses show larger adjustments for earlier adopters and for users with lower pre-adoption intensity. The contribution is to distinguish ecosystem level effects within legacy translators from total translation time effects, to map the short-lived exploration window, and to document brand specific redistribution rather than broad expansion. The findings inform platform strategy and policy by clarifying how LLM adoption rewires incumbent digital utilities in a leading Asian market.

title: Intent vs. Practice: A Comparative Study of Sustainable Electronics Perception and Behavior Using Survey and Online Review Data
affiliations: Purdue University, Purdue University, Purdue University and Purdue University

detail.title: Intent vs. Practice: A Comparative Study of Sustainable Electronics Perception and Behavior Using Survey and Online Review Data
detail.abstract: The intention–behavior gap in sustainable consumption is especially visible in the electronics sector, where consumers frequently express strong environmental values that do not translate into purchasing decisions. This study examined that gap by combining survey-based perceptions (n=64) with large-scale analysis of 138,488 Amazon reviews containing sustainability-related content. Survey participants prioritized convenient return options, recyclability, and the use of sustainable materials, and reported a willingness to adopt eco-friendly practices when these options were easy to access. By contrast, online reviews focused primarily on affordability, convenience, and product functionality; sustainability was mentioned only when it affected quality or usability. Welch’s t-test and Mann–Whitney U-test confirmed significant differences between self-reported survey responses and consumer-generated reviews, and topic modeling showed that trust and transparency concerns were salient in surveys but largely absent from reviews. Together, these findings indicated that physical, informational, and psychological frictions prevent sustainable intentions from becoming routine behavior. Closing this gap requires embedding sustainability into core decision factors — affordability, reliability, and usability — so that eco-friendly choices become the default rather than an extra effort.

title: Psychological Self-Regulation and Consistency in Instagram Entrepreneurial Branding

detail.title: Psychological Self-Regulation and Consistency in Instagram Entrepreneurial Branding
detail.abstract: In the context of digital entrepreneurship, Instagram has become a primary platform through which entrepreneurs construct and maintain personal brands. Sustaining consistent branding over time, however, requires more than strategic planning; it demands psychological self-regulation in the face of cognitive, emotional, and social pressures. This paper examines the role of psychological self-regulation in shaping consistency within Instagram-based entrepreneurial branding. Drawing on self-regulation theory, self-determination theory, and digital self-presentation research, the study conceptualizes branding consistency as an outcome of entrepreneurs' ability to manage motivation, emotions, and identity alignment. The analysis explores how self-regulatory capacities influence content coherence, engagement patterns, and long-term brand credibility. By integrating psychological perspectives with digital branding literature, this paper advances understanding of the internal mechanisms that enable entrepreneurs to sustain authentic and consistent brand identities on Instagram, despite platform volatility and performance pressure.

title: CATBridge: Enhancing CVE-ATT&CK Alignment Capability in Low-Resource Environments using Professional Knowledge from LLMs

detail.title: CATBridge: Enhancing CVE-ATT&CK Alignment Capability in Low-Resource Environments using Professional Knowledge from LLMs

keywords: and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK)Knowledge-DrivenLarge Language Model(LLM)Knowledge Distillation

detail.abstract: Aligning Common Vulnerability Exposures(CVE) with ATT&CK is a crucial step in achieving active defense. Existing machine learning and deep learning-based methods have received attention due to their high detection accuracy and strong generalization capabilities, but they struggle to effectively capture the deep semantic associations between CVE and ATT&CK. Large language models(LLMs), with their ability to understand complex contexts, are poised to become the mainstream approach for CVE-ATT&CK alignment. However, in low-resource environments with limited computational resources and scarce labeled samples, although prompt-based methods can enable large-scale LLMs (such as GPT) to exhibit excellent performance, their high computational costs and low inference efficiency severely limit their practical application potential in CVE-ATT&CK alignment tasks. In contrast, under the same constrained conditions, small-scale LLMs (such as Qwen-2.5-7B), although they can adapt to specific tasks through fine-tuning and offer better practicality, are limited by insufficient understanding of professional knowledge, making it difficult to comprehensively grasp complex attack behavior patterns. To address this, this paper proposes a multi-stage knowledge enhancement framework called CATBridge, whose core lies in constructing a "teacher-student" large-small model collaboration mechanism, through three progressive stages of targeted data enhancement, domain knowledge enhancement, and reasoning knowledge enhancement, to gradually guide lightweight LLMs to complete CVE-ATT&CK alignment tasks. Experimental results show that the framework performs well in low-resource environments, with the deployed lightweight LLM (7B) achieving an accuracy of 83.55%, a 33.29% improvement over SOTA, and an average improvement of 46.24% compared to large-scale general-purpose LLMs such as GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1 (671B), and Qwen3 (235B).

title: Structural Power Index: Quantifying Innovation Velocity and Engineering Stability as Leading Indicators of Alpha and Drawdown Resilience
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Structural Power Index: Quantifying Innovation Velocity and Engineering Stability as Leading Indicators of Alpha and Drawdown Resilience
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces Structural Power Index (Ps) as a novel framework for analysing enterprise technology companies to identify leading indicators of hidden alpha and proactively mitigate drawdown risk. The Ps framework seeks to offer a structural corrective to lagging financial data that is typically used in traditional equity valuation models. We will demonstrate how the Ps Index offers a robust alternative method to identify hidden value and proactively mitigate drawdown risk. 

The proprietary Ps methodology synthesises three primary metrics: Innovation Velocity (V), the speed of engineering output; Engineering Stability, the ratio of potential revenue-generating work to maintenance work; and Entropy Gap (1-H), the measure of the strategic focus of the engineering efforts. By weighting the velocity of innovative output against the management of technical entropy, we identify a predictive metric for stock performance that consistently precedes financial reporting cycles. 

Through a longitudinal study of 10 enterprise technology firms spanning 2018-2025, we demonstrate that Ps successfully functions as a high-conviction signal which translates into real-world returns. Over the eight-year duration of the study, a portfolio weighted by the Ps Index delivered a cumulative outperformance of 1,405 basis points compared to the benchmark. We also detail how a Ps-tilted portfolio achieves a 51 basis point Sharpe Ratio efficiency gain compared to the benchmark. 

In addition to identifying hidden alpha earlier than traditional equity valuation models, the Structural Power Index also acts an effective risk-mitigation tool. This is evidenced during critical downturn years where the Ps-tilted portfolio experienced a lower drawdown than the benchmark. 

Our findings suggest that technical entropy is a terminal leading indicator of impending valuation decay, while Structural Power is a prerequisite for sustainable alpha. By shifting the analytical lens to underlying engineering metrics, investors can consistently identify fragile value traps and capture resilient growth before it is fully priced by the market.

title: The impact of dynamic asymmetric activity on the evolution of cooperation
affiliations: Guizhou University of Finance and Economics, Guizhou University of Finance and Economics, Guizhou University of Finance and Economics, Tianjin University of Technology and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The impact of dynamic asymmetric activity on the evolution of cooperation

keywords.keywords: Evolution of cooperation；Dynamic asymmetric； Aspiration； Strategy stickiness

detail.abstract: To characterize the evolution of cooperation in real-world scenarios, this paper develops an evolutionary game model with dynamic asymmetric activity. In the model, individuals are classified into leaders and followers according to the comparison between their strategy persistence 𝜀𝑥 and the threshold 𝛽, and each individual’s node (influence) weight 𝑤𝑥 is adjusted adaptively based on whether the realized payoff meets the individual aspiration level 𝐴𝑥 . Importantly, leaders are allowed to incorporate their node (influence) weights 𝑤𝑥 into fitness evaluation, whereas followers rely solely on payoffs, which induces a role-dependent and dynamically evolving asymmetry in effective competitiveness. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations show that this mechanism substantially promotes cooperation and mitigates spatial social dilemmas. Micro-level analyses further reveal that cooperation enhancement requires the coordinated emergence of leader cooperators and follower cooperators, which together suppress the spread of defection. Moreover, the statistical results indicate that the facilitating effect of cooperation is not strictly positively correlated with the heterogeneity of node-weight. At last, robustness tests across different dilemma types, network topologies, and strategy update schemes confirm that the main findings remain qualitatively unchanged, demonstrating the generality of the proposed mechanism. These results provide a  parsimonious framework for understanding how dynamic asymmetry can reshape evolutionary pathways  toward cooperative behavior.
